items.body: Music fans will get their chance to start the season early, as this Friday is not only the first major release day of the fall, but another Bandcamp Friday. The fall season is incredibly frontloaded, and we suspect that some wallets (or Venmo accounts) will be emptied by the end of the week. We’re always excited about the Fall Music Preview, as many of us are summer people, yet it reminds us that there’s still plenty to look forward to. For now, it may still be warm, but pumpkin lattes and jack-o-lanterns are right around the corner. As the night continues to encroach and the leaves begin to turn, these are the albums that will accompany the transition. We wish all of our readers an amazing autumn! Our cover image comes from Seulement la Nuit’s Landscapes, covered below. William Basinski returns with a spacious, single track piano album, inspired by past-life regression hypnotherapy. Passing the Cup of Sorrows is slow and thoughtful, making a perfect accompaniment to meditation (Temporary Residence Ltd., October 23). Happy 10th anniversary to Slovakia’s mappa label, which celebrates by releasing a double cassette of 57 songs by 51 artists, including Lau Nau, Natalia Beylis, Alexandra Spence, Cheryl E. Leonard and so much more! Synthetic Water Music is the descendent of 2023’s Synthetic Bird Music, and they make a lovely couple (September 10). Fohn‘s Porcelain is filled with field recordings and tape crackle, which surround tender ivory melodies, specifically designed to imitate a late summer’s day. Conversation unfolds as a lawnmower kicks into gear; someone is still working! (Odda, September 11). Ned Milligan‘s Real Fun is a family affair, reflecting the joys of fatherhood via little moments: a bout of laughter, a downpour, a walk in the field. Lake Mary, M Sage and others make guest appearances (Florabelle, September 18). The same day, the label releases Billy Gomberg‘s pensive capacity, whose “one from october” is tailor-made for the upcoming season.   Difficult Art and Music introduces the season with a release for all seasons; Lille & rsn‘s The Diversity of Nature runs the course of the year, beginning with “The aspects of the seasons,” and is a collaboration between a composer and his 10-year-old daughter. Elfed/Elmet is a Welsh language “speculative history” from CIGFA/SEGFA featuring track titles like “Gwgddarylenogwernefiniog.” Both are out September 4.   Gilroy Mere could have died last year, but thankfully survived. While traveling back and forth from cancer treatments, he spent time making music, inspired by the paintings of Ravilious. Now in remission, Oliver Cherer is back on tour, and Furlongs is his grateful testament (Clay Pipe Music, September 4). Lynn Wright layers pensive guitar phrases on Before the Sinking Plains, adding wordless vocals and synth. The original loops provided solace during a long neurological illness, and now they are offered to the world in beautifully enhanced versions (Miasmah, September 4). Sadly, trumpeter Jon Hassel passed away before the last piece of Pentimento Trilogy could be published. Music Is Invisible, offered separately or as a three-part set is out October 2 on Ndeya.   Deniz Cuylan‘s For Luca is a tribute to a canine companion, sadly departed. In processing his grief, the artist turns to a multitude of friends, who make comforting contributions through music and voice. The end result is more thankful than sad, a reminder of an interspecies friendship (Hush Hush, September 18). Kjetil Husebø‘s Contours of Texture was also recorded during a time of loss and grief, and slowly crawls its way into the light (September 11). Noir Age has two releases planned for September 11. Night Foundation‘s Mental Objects is a meditative set billed as a sound suite, while Anasisana‘s Self Exploration is a Tunisian exploration of grief and its aftermath. On With What Little Light There Is Left, Matthew Paul Menovcik also addresses grief, highlighting the trajectory of healing (September 25). The prolific Home Normal imprint launches its fall season with two new albums. maps and diagrams‘ returning light is soft and hazy, tumbling like dust in sunbeams. midorinozu‘s lost horizons makes a fine companion, with a slight Midwestern flair. Both are out on September 4. And be sure to check out the places we carry, a nearly two-hour mix of new and unreleased selections, generously set to Name-Your-Price and released in early August.   Lamin Fofana delves into the Black experience on Corps Perdu, which “transmutes the words” of Aimé Césaire and others into sound. The result is both centering and informative (Shelter Press, October 16). Field recordings become elements of composition on Timothy Fairless‘s Friction, enhanced by wordless vocals and a sense of endless space (Dragon’s Eye Recordings, October 2).   Seulement la Nuit‘s Landscapes has been revealed one track at a time over the course of the year. On September 25, the full album will finally become available. We’re partial to Everything Fades Beautifully, as if perfectly reflects the sentiments of this time of year. Rachaell Lavelle guest stars on Eyes Bright and Low, a gorgeous album from Francis Harris & Gareth Quinn Redmond that crashes like light waves on an autumn shore (INNI, October 16). Minimal piano becomes even more minimal on Raphael Loher‘s Figuren. Originally played only for a small group of friends, these sounds were then deconstructed even further, resulting in a series of tone poems (Präsens Editionen, September 4). Dedekind Cut completes a trilogy with Dede-K-Ton, concentrating on cascades of piano. The dearly departed Ryuichi Sakamoto appears on two tracks (God Tier Virgo / Ojas Music / The Vinyl Factory, September 22). Here’s an interesting concept: an album comprised of time-stretched samples from Australian jazz luminaries. Danny Barwick brings new appreciation to these pieces by exposing them to an entirely new audience. home (fragments) is one of the first singles (Amica, September 22). IKSRE (I Keep Seeing Rainbows Everywhere) is preparing to release in all her forms (sound meditations volume 2), a sound bath that travels from “coral seas” to “falling snow” (Constellation Tatsu, October 6). Philippe Deschamps is fascinated with wind. The opening track on the artist’s last album was “The Wind’s Unseen Lines,” while the new set is titled Wind Paths. The music is gentle as a light breeze, the antithesis to a heavy gale (September 25). Matthew O’Neill honors avian collaborators on Through to Us, identifying a host by name: Ovenbird, Redstart, Eastern Phoebe. The field recordings are as important as the music, or even more so; the album unfolds like a conversation, reverent and true (Panther Mountain, October 16).   Thomas Guistini is releasing the ambitious COMPOSITIO on October 9: seventeen pieces, each accompanied by a video to eventually comprise a feature film. The first are already available for preview (EGEA). Reflections is the first taste of Mathias Villard‘s Past Radiance. The EP comes with a rework by Joachim Spieth, producing anticipation for the full set (Affin, September 4). Max Devereaux & Alec Watson‘s Febrile offers physical and psychological refuge. Recorded on the sixth floor of a skyscraper apartment while ICE raids took place on the streets below, the music vibrates with indignation and tension while proposing a more merciful path (Dragon’s Eye Recordings, September 4). Junge Eko‘s Pierced is a reflection of emotional rupture, translated into sonic form. Thanks to occasional vocals, the music often recalls the timbres of Codeine or Low (Warm Winters Ltd., September 4). Open to the Sea (Enrico Coniglio, Saverio Rosi and Matteo Uggieri) return on the impressionistic Beyond the Emotional Flood, a guitar-drenched narrative that seeks to lighten the weight of a difficult journey (Secret Lovers / Silentes, September 16). A single piece in seven movements, The Sky Was Out of Tune is a mesmerizing studio version of a live performance from Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok. The tones undulate and shift like clouds on a changeable weather day; one never knows what shape will form next (Morr Music, September 18). Built on a blue palette, Orkun A.‘s Dew is designed as a soundtrack for early mornings, when everything is new and the day is filled with promise (FUU, September 25).   Lost Tribe Sound’s Moss & Melee series is drawing to a close. The soft timbres of the dead bell reflect the nature of civic hall, a duo comprised of Craig Tattersall and Euan Alexander Millar-McMeeken. Their sound is restrained and intimate, awash in muted hues as the turquoise-tinted video for “woven dust” (October 2). Darkness Is Just Darkness, say Euan Alexander Miller-McMeeken & Henrik Meierkord, decorated ambient passages with spoken word, meant to console and surround. The cello is a steady companion, waiting in the wings (Audiobulb, September 22). Meierkord also guest stars on Trem 77‘s Textural Colour Spectrum Sandpainting, his treated strings shifting said spectrum from ambient to modern composition (September 1).   Windy & Carl Meet Optigan Conservatory is a duo of duos, four friends who have known each other for a long time and are finally getting the chance to record together. Piano, synth and guitar notes waft through the recording room, aloft on soft breezes, taking a while to settle on the floor. The comfort level is high, between performers and between performers and audience (kranky, September 4). After scoring Star Wars: Ahsoka and Dark Winds, saxophonist alas, i am myself (Deana Kiner) releases in the forest you’re still short, but you will grow, whose track titles are just as intriguing as those of the album and moniker (November 6).   Michael Scott Dawson will release a pair of peaceful guitar albums on September 4. Long Slow Distance sounds just like its title, perfect for an interstate drive, way past the comforts of civilization. kitsune no yomeiri delves into more Western timbres, despite its cover art and title. Every so often, the skies open for a swift shower (We Are Busy Bodies, September 4). Constellation is dropping three albums September 25. Steve Bates‘ Infinite Antenna is wobbly and warped; form dissolves into abstraction, song into texture. Courant Zéro‘s Solari is a guitar driven odyssey that occasionally borders on drone, while Light Conductor‘s Sequence Three lands between genres and will be covered later this week.   There Is Wonder Here, proclaim BJ Cole & Seconds. Their shimmering album is awash in pedal steel, Cristal Baschet and reverb, perfect for those sprawling late summer and early autumn days (Centripetal Force, September 18). Pedal steel is also the star of Luce Mawdsley‘s Dream, Baby Butch, an EP composed for the film “Catherine Opie: Moments of Being” (September 4). Chihei Hatakeyama and Ken Ikeda join forces on The Empty Rose, an elegant novel unveiled in sixteen chapters. The music drifts, descends and occasionally clings, producing a sense of unease (mykesrhiza, September 19). Blue Chemise‘s loop-based Mothers of All is haunted and haunting, a dark set for the darker months. Billed as “spectral salon music,” the score-like melodies stick in the head like buried traumas (Students of Decay, October 2). Texture reigns supreme on Vitor Joaquim‘s spacious Calligraphy, whose titles include “Oxygen,” “Carbon,” “Hydrogen” and “Nitrogen,” concluding with “Dust Stars.” One for the science fans! (October 20).   Kenichiro Isoda‘s Epilogue lies at the intersection of new age and ambient, while straddling the organic and electronic worlds. The artist has been active for over 40 years and has found his way to peace (Oath, October 30). Based on a sound installation, Brian House‘s Synchronizing Uncertainty introduces 286 circuits that “activate spontaneously, but may also be triggered by movement.” The result is a mixture of the planned and spontaneous (LINE, September 18). David Wunder Brägger mixes vintage organs with handmade electronics and more on Séance of Sleep II – La lévitation de Shéhérazade. A very cool double-sided art print is available for purchase, emphasizing the sci-fi aspect of the release, as seen to the right (Tiki Parlour, September 18).   Gorgeous electronic tones percolate throughout Pozo de Aqua, the upcoming album from Le Motel. Water flows, light twinkles and the set is infused with a sense of calm (Constellation Tatsu, September 15). What could be as peaceful as a seascape? Maxime Denuc‘s ocean-minded Club Imperiale is an invitation to stretch the former season as far as it can go (which is some climates is pretty far). The album operates as an electronic church, as techno rhythms are filtered through organ, producing a unique sense of uplift (light-years, September 11). Loop Diary incorporates field recordings in Music from Tokyo / New York, one city for each side. Subdued electronic rhythms lie underneath like the pulses of the cities. Given the choice of location, which side will players turn to first? (Personal Affair, September 14). Richard Allen

items.body: It will be released through Ideologic Organ next month Kali Malone has shared details of a new album, titled Burning Song. Marking her first LP of solo compositions since 2024's All Life Long, the new LP takes in seven tracks. items.body: Review by Progfan97402 — Melange was a two album wonder out of Spain. Viento Bravo is their second album and their final one. While their debut is good it suffers from the usual double album filler syndrome towards the end. Viento Bravo has none of those issues. This one was released on the now-defunct Beyond Beyond is Beyond Records, this is the same label that gave us the wonderful Japanese Canterbury band De Loreans. This is one seriously retro album where they even recorded with authentic recording equipment and gear, sort of like those artists who recorded at Toe Rag Studios in London, but this was recorded in Madrid. How to describe this? It's clear there's a psychedelic vibe to it but the prog elements are there. It makes me think of Magick Brother and Mystic Sister but without the female vocals or Canterbury influence even though Melange predates that band. The vocals are all in Spanish. The album starts of with the truly wonderful "R�o Revuelto", a wonderful and lively number. It's amazing I'm hearing this and it's from 2017. "Cheroqui" looks like it's the Spanish spelling of the Native American tribe Cherokee although you won't find any Native American influences in the music, although I'm not sure about the lyrics as the album never had the printed lyrics and I don't know Spanish. "Cotard" has a bit of that Spanish/flamenco feel to it, it also has a bit of that Middle Eastern feel as well. "Armos Preparadas" is just an amazing piece that simply blows me away. "Splendor Solis" is the closing piece and the lengthiest. This one has a bit of that Santana-like Latin American feel to it where the music goes into precision overdrive and speeds up towards the end. This is truly one of the finest albums I have ever heard that absolutely no one talks about. The only thing likely preventing a wider audience is the language barrier but I have never let that get in the way. Truly an album not to be overlooked.

items.body: Review by Matti — Firstly I feel appropriate to say I have reviewed quite many albums of Karfagen and other Antony Kalugin's works over the last ten years or so, giving several full ratings. Including OMNI (2025) to which this new release is a sequel. By my 4 stars I am actually NOT suggesting this wouldn't be equally good. Maybe it's just that it all has become a bit too familiar by now, lacking of truly new ideas. But judged on their own, all latter-day Karfagen albums are pretty excellent, tradition-faithful, wonderfully played & produced symphonic prog with both bombast and delicacy, and a certain pop accessibility. Perhaps OMNI II is slightly more operatic (partly due to the cast of vocalists) and intensive, be it a good or a bad thing. The majority of the instrumental pieces are placed on "Side C - Bonus Chapter", which in itself is a bit unnecessary and pretentious move. I think a more balanced running order of passionate vocal tracks and (usually more sensitive) instrumentals would have done good for the whole. Take for example the row of female-voiced, power-poppy 'Shadowbound', 'Shape of Love' sung by Marco Gluhmann (SYLVAN), 'Carry On' sung by Yogi Lang (RPWL) and 'Beyond the Mirror' sung by Per Malmberg (SALVA). The impressive guest list continues on the instrumental pieces where musicians such as the multi-instrumentalist Rob Reed (MAGENTA et al.), soprano saxophonist Marek Arnold and flautist John Hackett get their spotlight moments. Classic prog artists useful as Karfagen references include Steve Hackett, Genesis and Camel, and of the newer generation especially The Flower Kings and Kaipa (yes, Roine Stolt is also featured here) have the similar neo-symphonic approach.Kalugin's gift as a prog composer, keyboards player and producer is enormous. OMNI II is warmly recommended for any contemporary symphonic prog fans preferring fluent melodies and accessibility over experimental tendencies.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Simultaneously posted to my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights) with links for listening and purchasing.Today's album is slightly older than my more recent reviews, but certainly not an old album. Released on December 5 of 2025, "Elliptical Passage" is a collaboration between Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich (no relation to me that I am aware of). According to the press release I have received:Barry Cleveland is an LA-basedcomposer, guitarist, recordist,journalist, and author. His sevenalbums showcase a range of stylesfrom ambient to avant-rock to worldfusion. Cleveland also penned thecult classic book Joe Meek's BoldTechniques, and served as an editorat Guitar Player magazine for 12years. (barrycleveland.com)Robert Rich has released over 60albums across five decades,defining his unique language ofambient electronic music. Richbegan building synthesizers in1976, when he was 13, and laterstudied computer music atStanford's CCRMA whileresearching lucid dreaming. His allnightSleep Concerts have becomelegendary. (robertrich.com)Barry says the album began when he discovered some decade old recordings he had made. While improvised, he felt that the ideas had musical merit, and he contacted Robert Rich about using the recordings as a basis for an album, and he agreed. Recently, Barry reached out to me about reviewing this album, and I agreed. As always, I receive no additional compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Album credits:Produced by Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich.Mixed and mastered by Robert Rich.BC: Guitar, pizzicato arpeggione, bass, gongs, bowed cymbals, loopers.RR: Piano, flute, lap steel, percussion, Prophet X, Haken Continuum.All compositions by Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich.Primary guitar figure in "Zero of the Sanctified" derived from a line by Steve Rapetti. Track 1: Tangible Silence (6:55)This fades in with sustained synth chords, and swelling guitar notes. As it progresses, there are some interesting low pitched tones. The music gradually crescendos. There are no noticeable underlying rhythms. This might make a good meditation track. Various tones come in and out of the soundscape. At around 4:20 a flute takes the spotlight and most of the other sounds drop out. Different sounds gradually come back in. This reminds me of the introduction from Led Zeppelin's "In the Light". While this type of track is not in my usual wheelhouse, I can tell you that I enjoyed it and I found it to be well-done.Track 2 - Beckoning Voices (6:26)This one came so smoothly out of the first track, that I initially didn't realize that the track had changed. Once again there are long sustained sounds at first. However, a bass pattern begins to emerge, giving a sense of rhythm and momentum that the first track did not have. The overall sound, however, is still based on long, floating sustained tones. The music on this album, so far, would work as the soundtrack for a movie about space travel. The sounds are quite interesting and engaging. Later in the track, the bass pattern has dropped out, but the melodies are becoming more pronounced, with some subtle rhythms on piano. Intriguing track.Track 3 - Elliptical Passage (8:31)Once again, the transition from one track to another is seamless. A sound that makes me think of a spaceship enters the soundscape. This one feels more ominous than the first two. That said, there are some lighter tones in with the more foreboding ones. At around 3 minutes in, there are reverse recorded guitar sounds. Some harmonics are played in octave unison with a descending bass line after 4 minutes in. At around 6:45 there is a sustained guitar melody that actually reminds me of a melodi in Fleetwood Mac's everywhere. Another point of reference is that some of the sounds just before the eight minute point remind me of ones in Phil Collins' classic "In the Air Tonight". Track 4 - Gathering Stars (12:53)Once again, the transition is seamless. The guitar harmonics float on top of the sustained tones. The slide guitar notes are a recurring feature of the music. Some of the tones remind me of "In the Light" once again. I feel like we are about to "arrive" somewhere at about 8:30. This is becoming more intense as it goes along. The bass notes provide some tension and release. This is less melodic than its predecessor. The last portion has some hopeful sounding brighter tones. Track 5 - Luminous Expanse (10:51)As has been the case throughout, another seamless transition. The title implies sunrise over a wide, open area, And that is what the music implies to me as well as this track emerges. There is a subtle underlying rhythmic pattern on this one. The flute brings an organic touch to the soundscape. At around 6:40, there are some distorted power chords in the mix, but they are not the most prominent part. The guitar chords become more prominent at around 9:30. Track 6 - Zero of the Sanctified (9:30)As this one transitions out of the previous one, there are some clean guitar chords and a bit of smooth lead guitar phrases, but all still very sustained. The guitar is much stronger and more up front than it has been on the other parts of the album. This one is more horror movie soundtrack like than floating through space. The longer it goes on, the more disturbing it gets. The music calms down at around 5:30 and becomes more peaceful. The music begins to fade a bit with about one minute left, then some chime-ey guitar notes close the album out. OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:While electronic, ambient music is not really my favorite subgenre of prog, I can tell that Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich took great care in where every note and sound was placed on the album. The soundscapes are warm and rich. Fans of this genre will love this album. So, while it is not really an album that I will likely return to very often, I must reward the quality of it. I give it a 4 out of 5 stars. Or 80%. Many will rank it higher.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Black Bonzo's musical approach remains solid on this third album; vocalist Magnus Lindgren possesses a vocal timbre that suits the band's style perfectly, faithful to the Deep Purple mold as ever: raw, fast-paced, and relentless, yet tight and compact like Emerson, Lake & Palmer's Tarkus, driving forward and leaving nothing in its wake.Guillotine Drama is imbued with the epic feel the genre demands, and the interplay between guitar and organ is crucial. Furthermore, in keeping with the Swedish tradition, Joakim Karlsson is a meticulous guitarist, a virtuoso whose playing serves to propel the track forward. "Because I Love You" surprises with a more contemporary drum groove before kicking into a rock 'n' roll vibe with soulful vocals; there are psychedelic echoes and lingering traces of some members' previous band, Gypsy Sons of Magic.When "Zephyr" begins, I also detect echoes of Wishbone Ash in their prime, along with that rock sound featuring vocal harmonies. On "Sudden Changer," the string arrangements stand out, and the chorus adds a new layer of depth to the track; likewise, the acoustic feel works well to reveal a different soundscape on "War Machine," where the spirit of The Guess Who also seems to hover in the background.As the album unfolds, this "operations manual for the guillotine", subsequent chapters reveal a more inquisitive, subtle side of the band, employing a broader sonic palette. Following the welcome, breathless opening, "How Do You Feel" presents a ballad that is equally epic and melancholic, with a touch of darkness that adds a new dimension. That is, at least, until the rock kicks back in, reminiscent of the codas Paul Weller made his trademark in the 90s, and a glam atmosphere, albeit one that is dangerously wild and raw, once again takes hold of the band."Tell Me the Truth" also features a very unusual approach, both in the vocals and the use of the brass section, and Joakim Karlsson's solo is superb; for me, it is one of the album's most beautiful tracks. There is something unexpected in the twists and turns of its sound, which is intricate to begin with. "Supersonic Man" sounds raw and echo-laden; as this "guillotine manual" by Black Bonzo kicks off, one perceives less of the madness and mysticism found on their earlier albums, records that possessed certain edges this one lacks. Yet, as the tracks, or chapters, unfold, other facets emerge, crafted with the same passion, which more than compensates for any shortcomings. And then there is "Supersonic Man," where guitars and horns roar in a full-throttle farewell, complete with a funky final jam.If it sounds classic, it is because that was the band's intention; yet it doesn't feel like a copy, because it was created with a genuine desire to make that kind of music. That quality transcends the recording studio, even as it is captured within it.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — What I find interesting when listening to Mountains is, first, the use of folklore from regions bordering the band's native Finland, as if the depths of Nepal and the Himalayas were leading the way there, and second, how that same folklore lent itself, much like Middle Eastern traditions, to the sinuous, serpentine melodies characteristic of psychedelia; it is as if something ancient from the East were meeting the West to erupt into that invisible form of music. In this way, Hadal Sherpa immerses itself, with a synthesizer backdrop evoking outer space, in populating the soundscape with constellations, featuring guitar solos weaving between rhythm and lead parts, alongside a flute that highlights the desert-like, austere, and climatically violent and aggressive nature of their music. Goat Gaze will amplify these qualities with the captivating spell of a flute that dances over the psychedelic textures like a serpent.Starting with Dark Tides, one can find certain similarities to Hawkwind, yet Eastern time signatures are a constant presence, capitalizing on the sense of confusi�n, a kind of claustrophobia, arising from the relentless repetition of notes that shrink a space which, mere moments earlier, had seemed infinite.Upon listening to Ormus, one might even draw a parallel to John Zorn's Electric Masada, a comparison anchored here by the virtuosity of guitarist Vesa Pasanen. "Return to Farum Azul" breaks a certain stylistic monotony through the inclusion of a choir, lending the track an epic, palatial atmosphere."Mountains" and "Gurbet" resume the cosmic journey, drawing parallels with deserts and mountains, and that ascent into the infinite which serves as the album's central metaphor, with profound stylistic richness, though perhaps with an overly narrow focus on just one facet of that spectrum of possibilities.

"Breath
items.body: Review by alainPP — Long Earth offers melodic, smooth, and warm neo-prog?so accessible it feels like a sound you've heard before."Seahorses" opens as an instrumental, a cheerful neo-prog track driven by fresh keyboard sounds. The addition of Maaike shakes up the band's usual formula, bringing a fresh zest reminiscent of Mostly Autumn and Iona in a "soft fantasy" style; the synths evoke early Marillion, while IQ comes to mind during the building crescendos and intoxicating melodies. "Breathless" features crystalline, atmospheric keyboards?classic, contemplative, like gazing at Earth from afar?and vocals reminiscent of Ma�ko from Arrakeen, with a gentle voice flowing over the instrumentation. It is an airy, charming melodic ballad where rich synth tones meet a nervous guitar riff, ramping up the intensity much like Magenta's soaring passages. A languid, affectionate groove underpins the guitar solo. "Artificial Child" has a Beach Boys?or perhaps Fleetwood Mac?vibe; it's perfect for keeping the listener engaged, flowing as naturally as water from a spring. The melody is fluid and accessible?"easy prog"?while the ballad features sweeping vocals and keyboards. "Wanderlust" opens with an "Archangel"-esque feel (recalling BJH) before the keyboards shift the mood. It's a pop-infused track with a catchy, feel-good chorus and rich synth textures?a signature sound blending Genesis, Marillion, and Camel?evoking the Scottish landscape."Colours" is a multi-stage, sentimental neo-prog epic. It begins as an acoustic love ballad reminiscent of Anneke van Giersbergen (The Gathering), transitions into an energetic neo-prog surge of guitar, keys, and drums that dives into 80s nostalgia, and includes a velvety, languid keyboard break in the style of Marillion. Mike passionately showcases the breadth of his talent during an assertive crescendo that delivers nostalgia in spades. The finale sees a return to atmospheric acoustic sounds, with the vocals bringing the listener back down to earth. "Monochrome" features a riff clearly reminiscent of Led Zeppelin's "Kashmir"; the mood suddenly darkens, with vocals dissolving into a misty haze. A keyboard break evokes the Orient?melting electronic textures that repeat and then swell into a snarling riff?turning the track more solemn and symphonic. "First Casualty" boasts a focused groove and an easygoing piano undertone. It is a track of drippingly melodic pop-rock with a soothing, almost hypnotic harmonic quality, rescued by Renaldo's Gilmour-esque solo set against a cinematic helicopter soundscape. "Moon and Mars" is a vivid, crimson-hued nursery rhyme that sparkles brightly atop the arpeggios; featuring a melody worthy of the band Karnataka and led by Maaike, it tells the story of billionaires' voyages. The guitar solo sweeps away all resistance with its all-encompassing, contemplative melody; evanescent keyboards drift beneath the vocals?reminiscent of The Gathering?while crystalline acoustic and electric guitars blend to create a melancholic mood that gives way to an exuberant finale. "The Astronomer" is a bucolic, atmospheric ballad?accessible and an effortless listen. Instruments and lyrics gently intertwine, offering a shield against the destructive outside world. Keyboards deepen the pastoral immersion; while the synth break and the finale?featuring a lovely guitar solo?break no new ground, the track is best enjoyed simply as an anthem.Long Earth continues on its steady path?beautiful, yet conventional.

items.body: Review by alainPP — PATTERN-SEEKING ANIMALS, the up-and-coming band that could be considered the prog dinosaurs of the new millennium."Maybe All a Dream" features a cinematic, melting intro with ethereal guitar. The sound kicks in with Ted's expressive verse, still carrying that hint of YES, MAGELLAN. The wind and string orchestration evokes BIG BIG TRAIN. The track unfolds by revisiting genre clich�s, the finale surfing with a Gabriel-esque flute reminiscent of Neal MORSE; heavy stuff, well-reproduced. "A Flower Yet to Grow" follows the BBT formula, somewhere between neoclassical and contemporary prog metal, aided by the flavorful Mellotron and Dave's SQUIRE-style bass. The sudden break, as the name suggests, the somber keyboards, Ted's guitar proving he's a force to be reckoned with, and a melancholic, emotionally charged atmosphere. The finale showcases Ted's fingerwork and then his vocals, briefly on "Mystery"; the outro returns to? the intro. "Jade Sky" is an energetic mid-tempo track, an ethnic folk number with a Kansas-esque violin. The backing vocals add to make this track a popular and expressive radio edit. "Things I Don't Do" is a romantic ballad with John on vocals and piano, the choir soaring with captivating female voiceovers; a melancholic yet hopeful ode that soothes."Brea Away" expands with this long piece; a moment where I wonder about their sound: Spock's Beard, Yes, Neal Morse. We're in a nest of distinctive symphonic sounds; rhythm, melody, emphasis, and a barely concealed Olympian quality. The two-layered guitar solo propels the track to great heights, even if there's a hidden sense of repetition in the prog vibe. The finale soars even higher than the atmosphere. "Traveler on the Wrong Road Home," with its Southern trumpet intro, Ted belting it out, has the force of a KANSAS melody. A marshmallow ballad with a melting oriental violin over a spaghetti riff of furious trumpet, inviting you to sway languidly, breathing new life into the album. "Slowly Falls the Flying Man" opens with a dark and sober, medieval yet cheerful, undeniably reminiscent of KANSAS and STRAUSS. The solemn verse, set to a religious hymn, evokes the Middle Ages. The sublime symphonic drift, crystallizing the atmosphere, is a hallmark of MAGELLAN. Heavy stuff with velvety keyboards driving the rhythm, the catchy vocals on a sacrilegious mantra. A second break, this time with an electric pad riff reminiscent of Genesis, cements this album as a top pick of the month, culminating in a solemn finale with a will-o'-the-wisp flute descending from the heavens. "I Dream the World" closes the chapter on this bawdy tale, a pop-rock-jazzy ballad with a pleasing mid-tempo feel and a final, melting guitar solo. Simple but well done.PATTERN-SEEKING ANIMALS continues to leave its musical mark on the progressive scene with a sound that is consistent, cohesive, and enjoyable to listen to, with that little something extra that makes the time fly by. (4.25)

items.body: Tuğçe Şenoğul Atlas self-released There’s precious little information in English about Turkish vocalist Tuğçe Şenoğul. Aside from references to her time as one half of Seni Görmem İmkansız, and a few scattered write-ups about various collabs, it’s hard to find much reliable on the Istanbul-based artist. With that said, her streams on Spotify and Turkish language coverage certainly attest to some degree of popularity in her home country, with her new album Atlas (following from EP of the same name a few years back) demonstrating an intriguing mixture of modern electropop and traditional folk music. How that works in practice is fairly straightforward; on tracks like “Serseri” and “Cennet” Şenoğul mixes smoky, trip-hoppy production with strings, percussion and horns, all blended with a remarkable smoothness that speaks to the overall earthy and organic vibe of the compositions. Not every track relies on the mixture of traditional and electronic instruments – the lovely opener “Kırık Hikaye” is entirely made up of electronic ambiences, while “Bu Gece” is largely a simple piano based composition – their deployment a testament to the more measured and sensuous vibe of the instrumentals. It’s of course easy for the non-Turkish listener to get caught up in the novelty of hearing these sounds and musical approaches brought together, but there’s actually an interesting tension in how complex the arrangements and songwriting performance are, and Şenoğul’s presence as a vocalist. The record is very much at its best when the instrumentation gets out of her way and lets her take all the focus. The title track features a lovely mixture of percussion and some very interesting stringed instruments along with its throbbing electronic pulse, but it’s all about hearing how she slides between each different element, forceful without needing to belt it out or even change the urgency of her delivery. The tracks with a slightly more traditional structure end up being a mixed bag; “Sensin Bunlara Sebep” is a more traditional pop take on Turkish folk but is far less intriguing than the loungey, Collide-esque sounds of “Hatıramızla”, delivered with a reserved but coy wink. While you’ve got a few tracks in the mix like “Aşk Deli” that could fit on a darkwave dancefloor alongside Kite, the real appeal of Atlas lies in its warm, enveloping production and the power of Tuğçe Şenoğul as a performer. Even without knowing a lick about the themes and topics of these songs, she cleanly communicates love, sorrow, loss and resolve, picking her spots to hold back, where she employs her full range, and knowing how each bit of phrasing and inflection effects the whole. Buy it. Atlas by Tuğçe Şenoğul The post Tuğçe Şenoğul, “Atlas” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: I walk through fire with my head held high Is that really such a crime? Leaving a faith can redraw the borders of reality. Certainties that once governed time, guilt, desire, and the fate of the self fall away at once, leaving freedom inseparable from vertigo. A person must decide which pieces of the old world deserve burial, which can be carried forward, and how to inhabit a life no longer mapped by inherited answers. Portland post-punk quartet Nyx Division enters that exposed territory with By Design, a new single rooted in vocalist Domino Monet’s experience of escaping the Mormon church. Released ahead of the band’s East Coast dates, including a set at NYC’s A Murder of Crows, the song follows the collapse of a prescribed worldview into the frightening, sensuous freedom of choosing what comes next. Monet describes the subject as “the liminal expanse between awe and terror,” where ontological loss meets the exhilaration of reconstructing a world from its broken pieces. By Design opens with acoustic guitar and a dry, vibraslap-like rattle, setting a touch of spaghetti-Western theater ahead of Monet’s first lines. The full band soon bears down through Justin Cory’s heavy guitar figures and Mason Wilkinson’s firm percussion, while Alex Rivas sends a nimble bassline dancing underneath. As the initial force relaxes into a melodic groove, the track takes on a psychedelic hue. Cory’s guitar reaches toward the broad alt-rock and shoegaze sweep of bands like Catherine Wheel while retaining the core rhythmic pull of 80s post-punk. Monet supplies the song’s greatest sense of scale. Her held notes tremble with heat and conviction, drawing upon the commanding tradition of women rock singers from the 1970s and ’80s. Fire, memory, sin, and survival pass through the lyrics as lived conditions rather than decoration. The repeated title carries a productive reversal: language often used to justify a divinely ordered universe becomes a declaration of self-authorship. Design now belongs to the person who endured the old plan and walked away with the right to make another. That tension gives the track its lift. The music recognizes the cost of departure while making room for appetite, beauty, and volition. Its dance-floor momentum feels connected to the body’s return after years spent beneath doctrine, and its desert atmosphere suggests an open horizon where terror and possibility share the same immense sky. Listen to By Design below: By Design by Nyx Division Formed in Portland in 2021, Nyx Division brings post-punk, goth, and rock ’n’ roll into a muscular, romantic union. The group released the Dark Star EP in 2022, followed by the 2025 singles Soldier of Love and Midnight Lights. By Design expands that approach through acoustic color, psychedelic breadth, and a hard-earned sense of release. Nyx Division now heads across the East Coast for four early-September appearances. The band shares the Philadelphia, Worcester, and Cambridge dates with eX-Tradition. Their September 4 stop places them at New York’s Bowery Ballroom for the first of the festival’s two main nights at A Murder of Crows XI, appearing alongside Anja Huwe, Rosegarden Funeral Party, Creux Lies, and Guilty Strangers. Nyx Division East Coast Tour Dates September 3 — Philadelphia, PA — Cousin Danny’s Lounge, with eX-Tradition, NRG, and Subtle Body September 4 — New York, NY — Bowery Ballroom, A Murder of Crows XI September 5 — Worcester, MA — Distant Castle, with eX-Tradition September 6 — Cambridge, MA — Middle East Upstairs, with eX-Tradition Follow Nyx Division: Instagram Bandcamp The post “I Feel Like a Star Again” — Nyx Division Become the Architects of Their Own Destiny in “By Design” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.album: New Zealand Post-Punk Outfit Trauma Party Confronts the Political Circus in Fiery Video for “Roll Up (It’s the New Truth)”
items.excerpt: They’re bringing their violence They’re bringing their bile They’re juggling their words They’re bringing the new truth Trauma Party have found the right instrument for 2026: a busted carnival loudspeaker wired straight into the national nervous system. items.body: They’re bringing their violence They’re bringing their bile They’re juggling their words They’re bringing the new truth Trauma Party have found the right instrument for 2026: a busted carnival loudspeaker wired straight into the national nervous system. Roll Up (It’s the New Truth), the final video single drawn from the New Zealand group’s debut EP Because You’ve Been Good, barrels forward on rolling drums and blackened guitar, turning political disgust into a carnival bark that grows more feverish with every repetition. There is some of The Fall’s sour wit in the delivery, some Killing Joke in the pressure underneath, and a trace of Sham 69 in the gang-minded force of the refrain. Then the psychedelic stink rolls in. The Crazy World of Arthur Brown feels close at hand, while the guitars occasionally carry the broad, wounded sweep associated with The Chameleons. Trauma Party throws these ingredients into a garage-rock furnace and lets the song stagger around like a circus tent caught in a riot. The lyrics present authoritarian politics as cheap entertainment turned lethal. A fat orange clown presides over cages, bile, violence, snake oil, obedient freaks, and language mangled until falsehood becomes official reality. The joke keeps curdling because the circus imagery is funny for roughly half a second before its implications land. Spectacle becomes governance, repetition becomes persuasion, and the crowd is expected to applaud while vocabulary itself is dragged behind the tent and beaten senseless. “This song is not quiet; it screams at us all to wake up and beware ‘the new truth’ and the surreality of alternative facts,” the band says. “It’s a fiery post-punk alert from the fringes, illustrating the strength of art and music as tools of resistance.” Buddy Olson pushes the point further with a statement whose terse menace could have been painted across a barricade: “The privileged are few. We have them surrounded. Don’t let them escape. Hold them accountable.” The accompanying video gives the song an appropriately lawless setting. Filmed outside The Woolshed, Trauma Party’s clubhouse at the Waiheke Dirt Track, the band perform beneath a cold moon amid fire, smoke, and Molotov cocktails. Cars continue passing in the background, an almost comic detail that makes the scene more disturbing: apocalypse as roadside attraction, fury blazing a few metres away while ordinary traffic keeps moving, while everyone is expected to call the wreckage progress again. There is a Mad Max quality to the imagery, crossed with the scruffy end-times fatalism of A Boy and His Dog, yet the cheap-thrills destruction carries political purpose. Watch the video for Roll Up (It’s The New Truth) below: Trauma Party closes their EP Because You’ve Been Good by making the circus grotesque, psychedelic, and dangerously catchy. The tents are up, the clown is talking, the audience is already inside, and somewhere behind the music somebody is selling the lie as admission price. Listen to Roll Up (It’s The New Truth) below and order the single here. items.album: Tomorrows Letters release ‘Up Against the Wall’, the first single from a debut album
items.excerpt: Minsk-based project Tomorrows Letters released the noir synthpop single “Up Against the Wall” on 31 August 2026, the first track lifted from the debut album Kiryl Karotki plans to issue this autumn. The self-released single runs to three versions on streaming services, the original at 3:46, an extended version at 4:26 and a 2:54 remix by the Belarusian post-punk band Nürnberg. The Bandcamp edition pairs the original with the extended version. Karotki records Tomorrows Letters alone.
items.body: Minsk-based project Tomorrows Letters released the noir synthpop single “Up Against the Wall” on 31 August 2026, the first track lifted from the debut album Kiryl Karotki plans to issue this autumn. The self-released single runs to three versions on streaming services, the original at 3:46, an extended version at 4:26 and a 2:54 remix by the Belarusian post-punk band Nürnberg. The Bandcamp edition pairs the original with the extended version. Karotki records Tomorrows Letters alone. Nürnberg’s sound engineer Andrei Bobrovka mixed and mastered the track, and Karotki produced the cover artwork. The three versions run to 11 minutes and 6 seconds in total, and the release is out on Bandcamp and Spotify. Up Against The Wall by Tomorrows Letters What Tomorrows Letters says about ‘Up Against the Wall’ The song stages an internal trial in which the accused and the judge are the same person. Karotki explains what the arrangement is built around before the lyric reaches its closing line, “I’m a prisoner of my own mind”: “The song describes a state where your own mind acts as both the prosecutor and the judge in a trial that never ends. It’s about being your own worst enemy, trapped in a loop of self-judgment where conscience acts as a punisher rather than a moral guide.” A saxophone-like drone opens the recording before a mechanised groove takes over. Sparse piano notes sit next to Karotki’s measured vocal, and trip-hop menace and industrial textures run through the rhythm alongside the darker electronic pop of Depeche Mode‘s 1990s and early-2000s records. The saxophone returns between verses, winding through organ-like keys and a low electronic buzz, and the clipped construction carries the same severity as 1980s minimal synth. The lyric keeps to the courtroom setting throughout. Past mistakes supply the testimony, the mirror holds the verdict, and the heartbeat keeps time for the fear. Inside what the song calls the courtroom of the soul, the singer takes every role and pays every toll, until the line between right and wrong turns into another form of captivity. The Nürnberg remix is the first of several guest appearances and collaborations Karotki has lined up for the album. About Tomorrows Letters Tomorrows Letters is the solo project of Kiryl Karotki, based in Minsk, Belarus. The project mixes minimal synth and New Romantic sources with trip-hop rhythm and industrial texture, and Karotki works to a hardware-only rule, building tracks on vintage samplers and drum machines rather than software. His writing returns to a fixed set of subjects: isolation, self-judgment, Jungian ideas about the hidden self, maladaptive daydreaming, compulsive creation, and victories that turn out to be empty once won. “Up Against the Wall” takes the second of those directly as its structure. The samplers and drum machines leave the recordings with a dusty, tactile surface. Karotki’s collaborators on the single come from the same city. Nürnberg, the Minsk post-punk band whose engineer Andrei Bobrovka mixed and mastered the track, also supplied the remix that closes the release. The project’s earlier releases, the singles “So Be It” and “Go For It”, went out the same way “Up Against the Wall” has, self-released through its own Bandcamp page and the streaming services rather than through a label. The three versions of the single split the material three ways. The original runs 3:46, the extended version stretches it to 4:26, and the Nürnberg remix cuts it back to 2:54 and carries a joint artist credit to Tomorrows Letters and Nürnberg rather than a remixer credit alone. “Up Against the Wall” opens the run-up to the debut Tomorrows Letters LP. No title, tracklist or release date has been announced for the album beyond the autumn 2026 window, and no further guest names have been confirmed.

items.body: Los Angeles synthpop producer Danz CM released the double single “A Violent Power” and “Bontempi Pop 3” on 28 August 2026 through Channel 9 Records, the label she founded and still runs. The two songs run 4:15 and 3:15, are digital only, and were both built on vintage hardware rather than software instruments. The release arrives six months after “MYTHS”, the instrumental album she issued in February 2026, and points at a larger record to come. Announcing the two tracks on Instagram, Danielle Johnson wrote: “Two bangers and a double single of sorts. You can only assume this means one thing: yes, that a greater body of work is on the horizon.” How the two Danz CM tracks differ “A Violent Power” was constructed entirely from analogue synthesizers and runs on a steady new-wave pulse, with bass and keyboard lines locking into a dance tempo. The lyric deals with giving in to an emotion strong enough to override judgment, and the arrangement tightens around that idea as it goes. “Bontempi Pop 3” takes the opposite route. A breakbeat carries trip-hop weight underneath an Italian Bontempi toy organ, whose chirps and squeaks run across the track from start to finish. The subject is time and the wish to slow its passing by staying inside the present moment. Live guitars, acoustic drums, motorik rhythms and layered vocals appear across both recordings alongside the synthesizer banks. About Danz CM Danz CM is the recording name of Danielle Johnson, born on 20 February 1989 and raised in New York’s Catskill Mountains, now based in Los Angeles. She works as a producer, songwriter, composer, singer and graphic designer, and handles writing, production, mixing and art direction for her own releases. Johnson began releasing music in 2010 under the name Computer Magic, taken from a line of Viv Savage dialogue in “This Is Spinal Tap”. The early self-released records “Spectro”, “Hiding From Our Time” and “Get a Job” appeared in 2010 and 2011, followed by “Electronic Fences” on White Iris in 2011, “Orion” on Kitsuné in 2012 and the “A Million Years / Another Science” single on Modern Records in 2013. Her music found an audience in Japan, where it was used in campaigns for Panasonic and Kewpie Mayo. In 2015 she started her own label, Channel 9 Records, initially in New York and funded with licensing income, and released the Computer Magic album “Davos” on it that year. The EP “Obscure but Visible” followed on 7 October 2016, the side project Cody & Danz with Cody Crump issued the EP “Only the Hits” on 14 July 2017, and the rarities compilation “Super Rare” arrived on 15 December 2017. The Computer Magic album “Danz” came out in 2018. In August 2020 she retired the Computer Magic name and became Danz CM. The first Danz CM album, “The Absurdity of Human Existence”, was released in 2021, trailed by the single “Idea of You” in December 2020 and by “Domino”, “Something More” and “I Don’t Need a Hero” in early 2021. “Berlin Tokyo Shopping Mall Elevator” followed in 2023, the krautrock-leaning “LÄRM! EP” in 2025 and the instrumental “MYTHS” in February 2026. She has also written for film, scoring “While Mortals Sleep” in 2022 and Gary Hustwit’s New York subway map documentary “The Map”, whose soundtrack Channel 9 issued in 2024. Outside her own catalogue she founded the print magazine, website and podcast Synth History in 2020, remixed Ladytron‘s “Tower of Glass”, and has toured in support of LCD Soundsystem and Ladytron. Channel 9 Records has been based in Los Angeles since 2021. “A Violent Power” and “Bontempi Pop 3” are the first new Danz CM songs since “MYTHS”. No title or date has been announced for the larger release she referred to.

items.body: Prague Gothic Treffen has become one of the fixed points of my year, and I think the reason has less to do with ritual than with continuity. I return to the same island, recognise many of the same faces, meet people I may not have seen since the previous summer, and yet the two days never feel interchangeable with what came before. Music is the reason everybody travels to Prague, but PGT has always understood something that larger festivals sometimes lose when they become increasingly efficient machines for delivering artists to audiences: a scene only remains meaningful when the people inside it still want to meet one another. The twenty-first edition, held on 28 and 29 August 2026, made that idea physically larger. Fuchs2 and Bike Jesus were joined by Vila Štvanice as a third full venue, which brought the programme to three parallel stages and 21 performances, eighteen of them Czech premieres and one a European premiere. The festival was sold out, and the expansion unquestionably gave the programme greater range, although it also made this the most physically demanding edition I have covered. The three spaces are close to one another on Štvanice island, but a short walk becomes something else when hundreds of people are moving in the same direction, rooms are full and another band has already started a few metres away. As a photographer, that changed my own relationship with the weekend as well. There were performances I watched but barely photographed because the light made meaningful pictures difficult, and others where the area around the stage was so dense that I simply stopped trying to move further forward. I understand that completely. The audience has paid to experience a concert, not to spend it negotiating a corridor for photographers, and I would much rather come home with fewer images than behave as though an accreditation places me above the people standing in front of me. PGT has always felt unusually clear about that hierarchy, and for me it is one of the reasons working there remains enjoyable even when the practical circumstances become exhausting. Friday: the Treffen part of Prague Gothic Treffen Friday was the more social half of my weekend, although I did actually begin by behaving very professionally and going straight to Kadeadkas. The Cologne band, founded in 2016, describe their own music as a mixture of the raw, clinical post-punk of the early 1980s, psychedelic elements and punk energy, which is quite close to what makes them appealing without reducing them to a period exercise. Their set had abrasion and movement rather than nostalgic neatness, with guitars that retained enough dirt to keep the songs unsettled and a rhythm section that pushed rather than simply supported them. They were a good first band precisely because there was no ceremonial sense of easing the audience into the weekend; the music arrived quickly, directly and with enough punk instinct to shake off the afternoon before the festival had really begun. Kadeadkas at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil CattaC shifted the atmosphere into considerably darker electronic territory. Jens Helmis and Christian Schinköthe describe the German duo through dark electronics and rock, and that combination explains why their material carries more weight than a purely sequenced club project without becoming guitar music wearing electronics as decoration. What I enjoyed was the tension between the solidity of the programmed structures and the vocals, which brought a much more human sense of damage into the machinery. There is a particular kind of dark electronic music that becomes less interesting the more technically immaculate it sounds; CattaC avoided that by keeping enough emotional grain in the performance, so the songs had shape and discipline without feeling sealed off from the room. CattaC at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Skelesys was one of the Friday performances I particularly wanted to include because his position between guitar music and club electronics is more interesting than simply calling the project darkwave. Born in Buenos Aires and now based in Berlin, Skelesys moved from the darker electronic and EBM-inflected Epsilon material towards a more explicitly song-based combination of synth-pop, post-punk and goth on the 2024 debut album “Fading Echoes”. That history could be heard in the way the set operated: rhythm remained central, but guitar texture gave the music a more tactile, slightly corroded surface, while the vocals kept it from becoming purely dancefloor-oriented. There is a melancholic pull to Skelesys that never quite resolves into romantic softness, and in the intimate space of Vila Štvanice that mixture of movement and introspection worked particularly well. Skelesys at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Darkways brought yet another version of guitar-driven darkness. The Barcelona band’s second album, “Rust”, came out in January 2026 and deliberately revolves around decay, ageing, impermanence and the erosion of identity, while musically combining darkwave and post-punk with rock, metal and synthesizer-based influences. The attraction is that those elements do not appear as separate genre markers that need to be checked off one by one. The guitars give the songs weight, the synths expand their atmosphere, and the melodic writing remains immediate enough to carry the audience with it rather than asking everyone to admire the production from a distance. There is a melancholy in Darkways that feels muscular rather than passive, which made the set easy to enter even when I was already starting to divide my attention between music, photography and the people appearing around me. Darkways at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil By then Friday had begun to do what Friday at PGT usually does to me: the timetable slowly lost its authority. I started meeting people I had not seen for months, then somebody else joined the conversation, then somebody I had not expected to see appeared, and the five minutes supposedly available before moving to another stage expanded into twenty. This is not an accidental by-product of the festival. The organisers explicitly describe the “meeting”, the Treffen, as the central thing they want to provide, with the three venues designed as spaces between which people can move, meet and mix rather than as isolated concert rooms. My Friday followed that philosophy almost embarrassingly well, because somewhere in the middle of all those conversations I stopped trying to win against the programme. One of the casualties was OH Madonna, and this is the one I genuinely regret. I had wanted to see them, but Vila Štvanice was already difficult to enter and the surrounding timetable simply made it impossible to be everywhere at once. The project is still relatively young and has been developing quickly through darkwave, coldwave and synth-led material, which made this one of the performances I was especially curious about rather than a band I casually sacrificed. Missing something you actually wanted to see is always frustrating, but I would rather admit that than pretend I meaningfully experienced a set from somewhere near a doorway. I hope there will be another chance somewhere on the road, because OH Madonna remain on my list. I did make it back for Black Nail Cabaret, and they again demonstrated why they have become one of the most distinctive visual presences in contemporary dark electronic music. Emese Árvai-Illés and Krisztián Árvai have worked as the Hungarian duo since 2008, and their sixth album, “Chrysanthemum”, pushed their characteristic “pop noir” language into material preoccupied with death, fear and the difficulty of letting go without sacrificing the seductiveness of the songs themselves. What I admire about them onstage is the intelligence of the imbalance between the two performers: Krisztián can remain comparatively contained behind the electronics while Emese controls the visual field with extraordinary economy. She does not need to move constantly, because one deliberate gesture, one change in posture or the way she holds the audience’s gaze can acquire far more weight when everything around it is restrained. The result is beautiful, but never merely decorative; the elegance contains a certain severity, and her voice is strong enough to make that tension audible rather than leaving it entirely to the image. Black Nail Cabaret at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Friday ended for me with Vomito Negro, which was almost the opposite proposition. The Belgian project was formed in 1983 and belongs to the foundational history of European EBM and industrial electronics, with a catalogue that has repeatedly moved between dancefloor pressure, ambient material, harsh vocals and more contemplative electronic forms. There is no need for a band with that history to imitate the surface vocabulary of contemporary dark electronics, and the set benefited from precisely that lack of anxiety. The machinery was allowed to sound like machinery, the rhythms had genuine physical density, and the performance carried the severe economy of music that learned long ago that atmosphere does not require endless layering. After an evening in which I had spent almost as much time talking as listening, Vomito Negro provided a suitably uncompromising endpoint. Saturday: this time I actually followed the music Saturday was deliberately different. I had done most of my catching up the night before, so I treated the second evening as the day for music, which meant considerably more movement between Fuchs2, Bike Jesus and Vila Štvanice and considerably less standing outside with people promising each other that a five-minute conversation really would only take five minutes. I began with Majo Polyak & Radmila Svensson, whose work sits on the border between dark electronica and art-pop and has developed through collaborations that often treat sound, voice and image as parts of the same compositional environment. Their 2023 album “Neverending Story” was followed by “Angles morts” in November 2025, again involving Svensson and spoken-word artist Paulína Feriancová. The set was considerably more energetic than the melancholy and layered studio material might suggest, with Svensson giving it a strong physical centre while the projections expanded and destabilised the stage around her. I particularly liked that the visual component never functioned as expensive wallpaper; it changed how the music was perceived, sometimes making the space feel intimate and at other times almost disproportionally large, which is exactly what good visual work should do. Majo Polyak & Radmila Svensson at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Panic Priest arrived with an additional point of interest because Prague was the European premiere of Jack Armondo’s Chicago project. Armondo’s “Once Wild”, released in August 2025, broadened the project beyond its darkwave foundations through glam, Italo disco, new wave and more overt guitar presence, while retaining the baritone voice and doomed-romantic character that have always made Panic Priest immediately recognisable. The set began with technical problems, which is never the ideal way to introduce yourself to a new continent, but the recovery was more interesting than a perfectly smooth beginning would have been. Once the machinery cooperated, the guitar gained increasing importance and the performance acquired a much stronger rock edge, while Armondo’s voice remained the central dramatic instrument. Instead of allowing the difficult start to flatten the show, he gradually converted it into momentum. Panic Priest at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil At El Ángel Exterminador, the visual impression hit me before I had time to analyse the musical one. The Berlin-based post-punk, darkwave and deathrock project consists of Alejandra Batalla on vocals, Ludo-Van on guitar and marZiano on bass, and its March 2026 album “Crónica” brings together new recordings with remastered material from the group’s earlier cassette period. The guitars and percussion were ferocious, but Batalla stood in the middle of that force in a red dress and with long black hair, looking almost like a priestess presiding over the noise rather than someone trying to compete with it. That visual authority would have meant little without the voice, and this was where the performance became genuinely impressive: she could remain audible, expressive and emotionally dominant against guitars capable of swallowing a weaker singer whole. The contrast between the elegance of her appearance and the physical aggression surrounding her gave the entire set unusual tension. El Ángel Exterminador at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Cryo required a factual correction before anything else, because the current configuration is no longer Martin Rudefelt with Torny Gottberg. In 2026 Cryo consist of Martin Rudefelt and Ville Hising, with Hising also known from Run Level Zero and as DJ Rauz; their first concert in this new formation took place only on 25 July at MiNi-festival in Genarp. What surprised me in Prague was how little sense of transition remained. The rhythm was hard, clean and extremely physical, the synth structures retained the mechanical precision Cryo have built over roughly two decades, and the lighting amplified that architecture rather than simply flashing over it. There was a great deal happening rhythmically, but the set never became cluttered, because each repetition seemed to accumulate pressure instead of merely repeating information. For a configuration still very new onstage, the chemistry already felt convincing and, more importantly, alive rather than cautiously rehearsed. Cryo at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Corlyx were among the strongest surprises of Saturday because the current full-band formation has altered the scale of what the songs can do. Caitlin Stokes and Brandon Ashley are now joined by bassist Davide Rocco and drummer Flow Toulman, and the new 2026 material has increasingly exploited that configuration: “Sweeter Than Blood”, “More Anarchy” and August’s “Your Heart In The Serpent’s Mouth” all lead towards a new album planned for early 2027. The guitars sounded huge without losing definition, the real drums gave the songs much greater forward force, and Stokes remained completely dominant at the centre of it all. She is visually striking, certainly, but what impressed me was how little the show depended on image once the band began playing; the music had enough weight to support every theatrical gesture. Corlyx have moved well beyond the limitations of being described simply as a darkwave act, and the combination of gothic atmosphere, alternative-rock muscle and melodic immediacy makes far more sense when heard at full physical volume. Corlyx at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Horror Vacui followed by stripping away much of that polished construction and reminding everyone where a large part of gothic music’s nervous system originally came from. The Bologna band describe themselves wonderfully as “punker than dark, darker than punk”, and their new album “Shadows Sanctuary”, released on 7 August through Artoffact, examines darkness as a form of protection against a culture of constant visibility and exposure. The philosophical starting point is interesting, but the immediate experience was much less abstract: screaming, guitars, drums and the kind of tightly wound aggression that makes the body understand the music before the intellect has any chance to interpret it. After several electronic sets, Horror Vacui felt almost cleansing in its refusal to smooth the edges. Their current material may have moved somewhat further towards atmospheric goth rock, but the punk impulse is still audible in the attack, and that tension keeps the songs from becoming museum-perfect versions of darkness. Horror Vacui at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil Then came Potochkine, and for me there was no real competition for the highlight of the weekend. I have seen Pauline Alcaïdé and Hugo Sempé several times, and I still never reach the stage where I think I have absorbed enough of what they do. Their 2025 album “Sang d’Encre” continues the duo’s peculiar collision of poetry, techno, EBM, darkwave and synthetic harshness, with a theatricality that never loses its intimate, almost confessional quality. Hugo can stand behind the electronics almost like an operatic figure inside dense smoke and brutal light, apparently holding the entire architecture in place, while Pauline converts that structure into movement. Her dancing is not choreography laid over electronic music; it seems to emerge from the rhythm itself, violent one moment, controlled the next, continually giving the impression that the body is trying to outrun whatever the music has set in motion. Every time I photograph Potochkine, I begin with the professional part of my brain switched on, watching the light, anticipating movement and trying to calculate where the next usable frame will appear, and every time I eventually realise that I am dancing almost as much as I am shooting. Their performances feel like contained explosions, or balls of fire, because the music underneath Pauline’s movement is actually extremely precise while everything happening above it suggests release, excess and the possibility of losing control. That contradiction is what makes them so addictive for me. The theatricality never becomes self-conscious, the aggression never eliminates sensuality, and the danceability never turns the songs into neutral club material. I could see Potochkine repeatedly and still leave wanting another set, which is probably the simplest explanation of why they were my PGT highlight again. Potochkine at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil I had hoped to catch at least part of NITE, but this became one of the points where the physical reality of the weekend defeated me. Vila Štvanice was so packed that entering and reaching a meaningful position became difficult enough that I eventually stopped trying, particularly after Potochkine had already taken most of my energy. The official timetable makes clear how compressed the second half of Saturday was, with Potochkine beginning at 22:15, NITE at 22:30 and The Danse Society at 22:50 in three different rooms. Sometimes the correct response to a festival schedule is simply to admit defeat rather than pretend that two songs heard from the back of an overcrowded doorway constitute a review. My final major set was Buzz Kull, Marc Dwyer’s Sydney-based solo project, which has been operating since 2012 at the intersection of darkwave, EBM, industrial electronics, minimal synth and synth-pop. The February 2026 EP “Deep Hate” pushed that language towards a particularly severe kind of industrial pop, built around propulsive rhythms and an atmosphere that remains detached and nocturnal even when the music is extremely danceable. Dwyer understands how much authority can be generated without filling the stage with movement; surrounded by smoke and very heavy light, he can appear almost statuesque, like somebody standing inside the machinery rather than in front of it, while small changes in posture or delivery suddenly alter the entire tension of the room. I have seen Buzz Kull before and that economy still fascinates me, because minimal movement does not produce minimal impact. He commands rather than chases the audience, and the resulting set was a beautiful, hard and appropriately exhausting end to my Saturday. Buzz Kull at Prague Gothic Treffen 2026. Photos: Karo Kratochwil What PGT gets right The practical difficulty of this year’s edition is real. Expanding to Vila Štvanice gave Prague Gothic Treffen a broader and more ambitious programme, but a sold-out festival across three stages also meant that some rooms became difficult to access, certain transitions took longer than expected and overlaps occasionally forced decisions I would rather not have made. I missed OH Madonna, gave up on NITE, photographed some bands far less than I intended and occasionally realised that I had barely found time to eat because I was moving between venues again. None of that, however, is what I will remember first. The greatest value of Prague Gothic Treffen continues to be its people, and I do not mean that in the vague festival-review sense in which every crowd is described as wonderful because nobody wants to insult the readers. There is something structurally different about the atmosphere here. People notice each other, help one another, make room and talk easily to strangers, while the organisers have made the principles behind that atmosphere unusually explicit: racism, homophobia, xenophobia, transphobia, harassment and violent behaviour are grounds for immediate removal and bans from future Sanctuary events. This year there were also people visibly available around the venues to help anyone feeling unwell or unsafe, and the bartenders and staff again treated safety as part of running the event rather than an inconvenience to be dealt with after something has gone wrong. What matters is that those policies rarely feel as though they are being imposed on a fundamentally hostile crowd. They describe behaviour that is already largely present among the people who come here, which is probably why Friday can disappear into conversations without feeling like time stolen from the festival. Those conversations are part of the festival. The organisers themselves say that while the line-up matters, the meeting is the point, and after attending PGT year after year I think that distinction explains its longevity better than any list of bookings could. There is already a reason to mark the next summer in the calendar. The poster displayed at this year’s festival announces XXII Prague Gothic Treffen for 27 and 28 August 2027, with the first four names confirmed as Dina Summer, Twisted Nerve, The Spoiled and HUIR, with more still to be announced. It is already a wonderfully strange cross-section: Dina Summer bring the dark-disco and synth-wave world of Local Suicide and Kalipo; the Edinburgh veterans Twisted Nerve connect PGT directly to the punk-to-goth transition of the early 1980s; The Spoiled represent a much newer Italian post-punk perspective; and Barcelona duo HUIR arrive after releasing “States of Light” in May 2026. That announcement felt like an appropriate way to leave Prague because PGT has never worked for me as a collection of isolated concerts. Friday was almost equally about people and music; Saturday was an intense sequence of performances in which Potochkine set the standard impossibly high, Cryo showed that a changed line-up can immediately find its own chemistry, Corlyx sounded bigger and more physical than ever, El Ángel Exterminador gave me one of the weekend’s most arresting visual and vocal performances, and Buzz Kull once again proved how much power can come from disciplined restraint. Around all of that were the conversations, accidental meetings, people dancing, people taking care of each other and the strange little community that reassembles on Štvanice for two days every year. That is why Prague Gothic Treffen remains one of my yearly traditions. I go there to work, I take far too many photographs, I run between stages, I inevitably miss something I desperately wanted to see, and at some point I put the camera down because the music is too good not to dance. What makes me return, however, is the fact that none of those experiences happen in isolation. At PGT, music still feels inseparable from the people gathered around it, and after twenty-one editions the word Treffen still describes the festival better than anything else. About Prague Gothic Treffen Prague Gothic Treffen is an annual dark alternative festival held on Štvanice island in Prague and run by the Sanctuary organisation. The twenty-first edition took place on 28 and 29 August 2026 and sold out. It ran across three parallel stages for the first time, with Vila Štvanice joining the existing Fuchs2 and Bike Jesus venues, and carried 21 performances, of which eighteen were Czech premieres and one a European premiere. The 2026 bill included Kadeadkas, CattaC, Skelesys, Darkways, OH Madonna, Black Nail Cabaret and Vomito Negro on the Friday, and Majo Polyak & Radmila Svensson, Panic Priest, El Ángel Exterminador, Cryo, Corlyx, Horror Vacui, Potochkine, NITE, The Danse Society and Buzz Kull on the Saturday. Panic Priest’s set was the European premiere of Jack Armondo’s Chicago project. The organisers publish a conduct policy under which racism, homophobia, xenophobia, transphobia, harassment and violent behaviour are grounds for immediate removal and a ban from future Sanctuary events, and staffed the 2026 edition with people available around the venues for anyone feeling unwell or unsafe. The twenty-second edition is set for 27 and 28 August 2027. Dina Summer, Twisted Nerve, The Spoiled and HUIR are the first four acts confirmed, with the rest of the bill still to be announced.
