items.body: August 14 - 16, 2026, Peitz, Germany Up a creaky set of wooden stairs to the lofts of the 1810 Huettenwerk of the historic Ironworks and Fishery Museum of Peitz, an imposing building full of old heavy tools for the iron foundry and fishing works in the surrounding carp ponds, is an exhibition on Free Jazz in the German Democratic Republic (former East Germany). It’s a traveling show, having accompanied Jazzwerkstatt concerts and festivals over the years. The first time I encountered it, at a Globe Unity Orchestra concert in Potsdam in 2014, it prompted me to dig for all of the Amiga Jazz records that I could find, leading to likely the most complete collection of East German jazz in New Jersey. Every year for the past ten years or so that I’ve been to the festival, I find myself drawn to the exhibition, like a pilgrim to worship. Each station of the exhibit offers a glimpse into this well documented but still mythical past, with a final station showcasing the Peitz Festival. Created in 1973 by two young free-thinking music fans, Uli Blobel and Peter “Jimi” Metag, both from the small East German town of Peitz, the festival drew other like minded youth to hear both East German musicians like Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky and Conny Bauer as well as West German musicians like Alexander von Schlippenbach and other musicians from the other side of the Iron Curtain such as Barry Guy and Wadada Leo Smith. The names are many and the history can be read in the “Woodstock am Karpfenteich’ books as well as experienced here , and the story is a good one. Lasting until shut down by the government in 1982 and restarted by Blobel in 2011 under much different conditions, the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz festival of 2026 still draws some of those who trekked by train and Trabi to the original, but is also working to draw in a new audience whose connection to the past is being built by heading to upper floors via creaky wooden stairs. Starting in 2024, Marie Blobel, the daughter of Uli Blobel, took over. Some of the changes Marie Blobel made included moving the festival from the center of Peitz to the grounds of the fishing museum amidst the carp ponds and injecting a festive flair into the weekend long event. With a packed schedule of concerts and a two kilometer hike to the Doener restaurant, festival goers are oriented to the wurst stand, the home cooked vegetarian dishes at the beer tent and the biergarten around the corner. Kids have the chance to make their own music with an imaginative looping station and everyone can climb aboard the “Karpfenbummler,” an electric miniature train that will take you in style from the festival to town to the train station. Coming into its own it the new form, Jazzwerkstatt Peitz was awarded the Deutsche Jazzpreis this past year. -- Gebhard Ullman’s Hemisphere 4 PLUS (biergarten stage) The concerts began on Friday evening with the folk-meets-modern-jazz sounds of Trio Ivoire . In the trio's music, Hans Lüdemann ’s piano and electronics and Christian Thomé 's percussion and electronics are met with the organic tones of Aly Keïta ’s balafon, an African instrument described as a “ a gourd-resonated xylophone .” The music is upbeat and highly syncopated and thus quickly had some of the at-capacity audience on their feet swaying to their rhythms. As soon as the set ended, the audience began shuffling off, around the museum and cycler hostel (the Gurkenradweg - yes, the Pickle Bikepath - passes by the festival grounds), to a biergarten, where a stage has been set up under a lush copse of trees. Woodwindist Gebhard Ullman ’s newest formation, Hemisphere 4 PLUS , featuring a mix of his current electric and acoustic groups, began with a chamber-jazz like combination of Anna Viechtl ’s harp and Taiko Saito’s vibraphone. Disrupted by a crash of percussion, the group tumbled into a pulsating groove. Describing the music as “sculptures,” Ullmann led the group through an alluring mix of the delicate (add Silke Lange accordion to the chamber jazz components), hard-hitting (with Eric Schaefer on drums and Oliver Potratz on bass) and other-worldly ( Liz Kosack ’s keyboard and synthesizer). OM (main stage) A short shuffle back to the main stage where OM , the legendary avant-jazz-rock group, were ready to go. The original group members, saxophonist Urs Leimgruber , guitarist Christy Doran and bassist Bobby Burri were joined by drummer’s Gerry Hemingway and Tony Buck who have replaced the late Fredy Studer, as they did on the recent Intakt release Suedpol . After a short freely improvised intro from Leimgruber, a blast of rock energy from Doran gave root to a swirling squall of tones and the music slowly evolved into a groove led by the two percussionists. Moments of electric Miles colored the rich panoply of sound which ranged from deeply experimental to outright rock. An excellent set. Closing out the main stage for the evening was the quartet Selvhenter from Copenhagen. Saxophonist Sonja LaBianca and trombonist Maria Bertel and drummers Anja Jacobsen and Jaleh Negari crafted a dark, throbbing techno-jazz designed to get festival goers on their feet. It was quite late by the time the quartet’s final notes faded, but the show wasn’t over … yet, as drummer Willi Kellers and organizer Wolfgang ‘Assi’ Gloede were hosting a jam session in the cozy workshop building behind the main stage. Amongst painted fish sculptures and some serious looking tools, saxophonist Lotte Anker , keyboardist Liz Kosack and bassist Reza Askari joined Kellers in free-jazz improvisation that began with electronic percolations and slowly crescendoing notes that eventually balled into an exciting and thorny tumbleweed of sound. Following the opener, Gloede curated combinations of professional and hobbyist musicians who improvised into the wee hours. -- Wanja Slavin (sitting far right) (church) Saturday’s full schedule began in the town church where saxophonist and festival Improviser-in-Residence Wanja Slavin , last year’s winner of the Brandenburg Jazzpreis - an award developed by Jazzwerkstatt and the state of Brandenburg - debuted a new composition with a band comprised of Peter Evans on trumpet, Leonard Huhn on bass clarinet, Almut Kühne with vocals and Kaja Draksler on piano. The rich 45-minute piece moved seamlessly between moods and approaches as darker moments were balanced by more hopeful passages. Repetitive arpeggios and prominent electronics formed a consistent tonal base accentuated by the dissonant church organ and several outstanding solos. A short while later back at the festival grounds, percussionist and singer Mariá Portugal’s EROSÃO septet took the stage in the rapidly heating up early afternoon. The music began with a brass fanfare as the group walked-on the stage and transitioned to Portugal singing over polyrhythmic accompaniment. Concentrated on a repertoire of songs that drew heavily on her Brazilian background, Portugal’s vocals took center stage, while the high-powered group of saxophonists Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier , trombonists Matthias Müller and Moritz Wesp , tubist Carl Ludwig Hübsch and bassist Reza Askari provided solid support. Afterwards in the Huettenwerk building, the duo of Mohammad Mostafa Heydarian and Valentin Portron , performing on the traditional Iranian tanbur and bendir - a stringed instrument and hand drum - continued the expansion of the festival’s musical purview. Impro-Concert: Tony Buck, Matthias Mueller, Taito Saito (workshop) Two improvisation sessions, tucked away in the workshop building, injected a bit of the unexpected into the afternoon. The first introduced the British woodwindist Tamar Osborn with the American bassist Nick Dunston and drummer Gerry Hemingway . This first meeting proved fruitful. Clicking quickly, Osborn leaned into the deeper registers of her baritone sax, while Hemingway contributed a lithe, but full, pulse and Dunston provided a melodically swinging bridge between the two. The later improvisation session joined three Berlin based improvisors who have been in each other’s orbits but never played together before. Vibraphonist Taiko Saito , trombonist Matthias Müller and drummer Tony Buck played a set ranging from contemplative to combustive. Aki Takase, Robert Landfermann, Christian Lillinger. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The mid-afternoon offered both unforgiving sun and an excellent set from pianist Aki Takase who was performing her upbeat, complex, and often humor-laced music with drummer Christian Lillinger and bassist Robert Landfermann on the main stage. The trio’s music is impressive, Lillinger, with his agitated, driving approach is a perfect rhythmic partner for Takase’s own intensity, and Landfermann’s rhythmic and melodic playing adds a nicely fitting layer. Nearing the end of the set, a dramatic moment ensured when Takase suddenly collapsed from the heat. Fortunately, it was reported that the pianist was already on the move to the next concert in Austria that evening. Darius Jones & Otomo Yoshihide Quartet. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix A little later the shows were back in the biergarten, where the trees provided some relief from the 100 degree heat, and the Czech quartet Edemit added a jolt of avant-rock to the day while Neiscer and Portugal picked up in a duo form the earlier set. As the day began to cool, the action moved back on the main stage where Darius Jones and Otomo Yoshihide (alto saxophone and guitar, respectively) augmented by bassist Nick Dunston and drummers Gerald Cleaver and Yasuhiro Yoshigaki provided an electric set. Following a rousing Coltrane-like introduction, the rhythm section gave Jones a rumbling foundation for his soaring melody to which Yoshihide responded with a feedback-laden solo, pushing the music to an early peak. The music ebbed and flowed, from dark atmospheric wanderings to high-energy free-jazz explosions over pulsating rhythms. Afterwards, the UK-based Ill Considered featuring Tamar Osborn ( Idris Rahman on saxophone, Liran Donin on bass, Emre Ramazanoglu on drums and Osborn with various woodwinds) closed out the night with a set heavy on beats and Middle Eastern-tinged scales. The set ended with about half the remaining audience dancing in front of the stage. -- Perhaps in normal times, it would have been a disappointment but after the previous day’s oven-like disposition, the cool, rain-soaked grey morning greeting festival goers on Sunday was welcome. A church service in the Huettenwerk started the day for the faithful while out on the festival yard, the others were huddling under the drink stand tents sipping coffee while the bratwurst man started up his grill. First musical act, Richard Koch’s Ray of Light was the only one to be seen under the steadily raining sky. They began with the trumpeter playing a regal anthem and launching into a cheery, melodic tune filled with the folkish sounds of Fabiana Striffler ’s violin and Valentin Butt ’s accordion along with the rhythm support of Andreas Lang ’s bass and Nora Thiele ’s frame drums. The “gute laune” (good mood) music with its blend of up-tempo jazz, classical and folk elements provided a lighthearted start to another long day of music. Their timing was perfect too, as Ray of Light reached the end of their set, the first beams of sun reached the festival grounds. Have You Ever Been Experienced. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The opening set was followed by Brandenburg Jazzpreis. Prize winner, guitarist Andreas Willers , who was to present his Hendrix inspired group Have You Ever Been Experienced , featuring a top-notch group of Berlin based musicians: Amy Green on vocals, Rieko Okuda on piano, Jan Roder on bass and Christian Marien on drums, was unfortunately too ill to attend. Despite this, the group, still gave a rousing performance, taking well-worn Hendrix themes and spinning them anew. Okuda took over the guitar solos with a distorted synthesizer, while Roder and Marien made sure the foundations were securely fortified. Most revelatory were Green’s vocals, which retained enough of the melody for song-recognition and enough improvisational liberty to free them from nostalgic interpretation -- for example, an updated interpretation of Allen Ginsberg’s Howl set to a free-jazz take of ‘If 6 was 9.’ The final two sets of the festival moved back into town to the church. The first was the Polish duo of vocalist Maniucha Bikont and bassist Ksawery Wójciński performing a set of haunting folksongs. Discovered through Bikont’s musicology research, the songs came from a disappearing tribe in the Ukraine, with themes that touched on the universal: suffering, responsibility and expecting better manners from the dead. Performed solely with voice and bass, the music filled the church mesmerizingly. Konradism. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The closing set to the festival may have also been one of the most anticipated. Connecting the festival’s eras, trombonist and archetype of the original Peitz festival and East German free-jazz in general, trombonist Conny Bauer presented the large group Konradisms with an extended composition of “chamber big-band” that mixed generous improvisation and dramatic riffs. Joining Bauer was a cross section of a younger generation of German-based musicians: Nils Wogram on trombone, Maxine Troglauer also on bass trombone, Gerhard Gschlössl on tuba, Claudio Puntin on bass clarinet, Maria Reich on violin, Emily Wittbrodt on cello, Matthias Bauer on bass, Dag Magnus Narvesen on drums and Rieko Okuda on piano. Often breaking into small combos - trombone and piano, tuba and violin - the solos would grow intense and eventually congeal around common themes. A stand out was Puntin whose bass clarinet playing ranged from the sound of a flute to deep, woody resonance. After an intense two and half days of music, the two last concerts were a satisfying and full-circle-moment ending to the festival. Overall, one could sense a tilt towards the new - nights that ended with experimental but danceable music, a series of risky but successful workshop concerts with musicians meeting for the first time, an infusion of world-music elements, and a loosening, but not denying, deference to the past, showing a way forward. More about the Peitz festival: Review of the 50th Anniversary Peitz Festival Review of the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz Boxset Jazzwerkstatt Peitz website . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Singapore's homegrown music scene will take centre stage this September as HOMEGROWN returns for its third edition, bringing together some of the country's biggest breakout acts and rising talents for a free three-day festival at Paya Lebar Quarter Plaza.

Taking place 11–13 September, the festival will be headlined by Regina Song and brb., two artists whose journeys from Singapore's bedroom studios and local gig circuit to international recognition have become emblematic of a new generation of musicians making waves beyond the Lion City.

Presented by the Music & Drama Company (MDC), HOMEGROWN has increasingly positioned itself as both a showcase of Singapore's thriving music ecosystem and a platform for emerging artists. This year's edition continues that mission with performances spanning indie pop, alternative rock, R&B and pop, alongside a youth band competition and booths spotlighting local creative businesses.

For Regina Song, the festival marks another milestone in what has been a meteoric rise. The Singapore singer-songwriter captured global attention when her breakout single 'the cutest pair' topped Spotify's Global Viral Chart, while amassing over 90 million streams worldwide. Her appearance at HOMEGROWN will also be her first public performance since releasing her latest album, everland.

"I'm so excited to be playing [in public] for the first time after releasing my new album," she shared. "Looking forward to seeing everyone again!"

Meanwhile, indie-pop trio brb. return home after taking their music across international festival stages and an extensive US tour. Having built their reputation within Singapore's independent music scene before finding audiences overseas, the band says returning to perform for local fans carries special significance.

"Homegrown [local] stages made us who we are," the trio said. "Playing this festival with our new songs, for our own community, we can't wait."

The pairing of Regina Song and brb. as headliners reflects the festival's central theme: celebrating Singaporean artists who have successfully built global audiences while remaining deeply connected to the communities where they first began performing. According to organisers, both acts represent a generation of musicians who found worldwide success through digital platforms before returning to support the local music scene that helped launch their careers.

Beyond the headline performances, HOMEGROWN 2026 will feature an extensive lineup of local acts across all three days.

Friday's opening night will begin with HOMEGROWN Rising, a youth band competition organised in collaboration with MOMENTUM, a music discovery and development platform that provides performance opportunities and industry mentorship for emerging artists. Eight bands will compete throughout the evening before the MDC NSF Band performs and winners are announced.

Saturday shifts the spotlight to Singapore's indie and alternative scene, with performances from Ice Cream Sundays, Dominic Chin, Forests, RINES, TP Music Vox and Khim Ng before brb. closes the evening.

Sunday continues with Ice Cream Sundays returning alongside Aaron Bunac, 10pm Noise Complaint, Izzathy Halil, TP Music Vox and Gail Belmonte, before Regina Song headlines the festival's closing set.

Running from 5:30 PM to 9:30 PM on Friday and from 2:15 PM to 8:30 PM across the weekend, the festival is free to attend throughout all three days. Festival-goers can also browse booths by local brands, highlighting Singapore's wider creative and entrepreneurial community beyond music.

items.body:
timelesz are taking their latest chapter worldwide. The eight-member J-pop group released their second studio album, MOMENTUM, on global streaming platforms on 31 August. The 17-track record is now available via Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, and more.

Built around a classic J-pop core while exploring different genres, MOMENTUM marks timelesz's second album with their current eight-member lineup. The record draws from the group's experiences over the past year, reflecting their drive to keep moving forward while holding on to moments from the past, present, and future.

Leading the album is 'GOOD TOGETHER', which arrived with an accompanying music video.

MOMENTUM also features 'Believers', the theme song for member Yoshitaka Hara's starring drama Yokohama Neighbors Season 2, alongside the group's first unit tracks. The units were formed based on overseas and creative assignments featured in timelesz project -REAL-, the follow-up docuseries to timelesz project -AUDITION-.

The unit tracks include 'No Map Just Vibes' by So Matsushima, Masaki Hashimoto, and Shuto Inomata; 'We’re on the Top' by Shori Sato, Yoshitaka Hara, and Taiki Shinozuka; and 'half & half' by Fuma Kikuchi and Takuto Teranishi.

The album closes with bonus track 'Akubi', which has also received its own music video.

The release follows timelesz's latest single, 'Kienai Hanabi (Timeless Fireworks)', the theme song for the animated film Kimi to Hanabi to Yakusoku to. The project marks Shori Sato's first starring voice acting role.

items.body:
ENHYPEN have reached a new career high. The K-pop group have earned their first No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with their eighth mini album, THE SIN : BLISS.

The record debuted atop the chart with 98,000 equivalent album units earned in the United States. Of that figure, 92,000 came from traditional album sales, while 6,000 were streaming equivalent album units.

The milestone follows ENHYPEN’s steady climb on the Billboard 200. The group first entered the chart at No. 18 with BORDER : CARNIVAL in 2021, before going on to secure multiple Top 5 releases. Both ROMANCE : UNTOLD and THE SIN : VANISH previously peaked at No. 2.

Beyond the US, THE SIN : BLISS recorded 2.09 million copies sold worldwide in its first week, becoming ENHYPEN’s fifth album to surpass two million copies in sales.

The achievement comes amid the group’s ongoing global expansion. ENHYPEN recently wrapped up the Latin American and US leg of their BLOOD SAGA world tour, which drew more than 193,000 fans across 12 shows in eight cities. This included a sold-out stadium show in São Paulo with a reported capacity of 41,000.

The group also made appearances at Campo Marte ’26 in Mexico City and San Diego Comic-Con.

THE SIN : BLISS marks ENHYPEN’s latest chapter in the cinematic storytelling that has become a defining part of their releases — and now, their first album to reach the top of the Billboard 200.

items.body: The year of blue continues: blue art, blue music, blue moods. Klara Lewis‘ Opening is an azure version of the hue, twisting and turning like permutations seen beneath varying degrees of light. The first single and opening track “Ta Min Hand” establishes the baseline from which the album will drift, like a small vessel upon the sea. Even the music includes waves. A sweet melody emerges, loops and abrades. In “City,” solo piano plays over the sounds of traffic and conversation, momentarily pausing as if to listen to the other acoustic sources. Suddenly a more aggressive set of sounds conquers the sonic field, a helicopter of rovers and gears. The piano reenters, insistent, then the conversation, posing questions about where the attention turns in an economy of sonic competition. The more orchestral “Vaknar” (“Waking”) attempts to soothe, but the ground has already proven unstable. The looping continues, but the volume increases. Opening revels in juxtaposition and incremental shift. “Feel” and “Drip” were composed for Mika Taanila’s expressive film “Failed Emptiness,” which toys with expectations of light. As the album’s most abrasive piece, “Feel” stands in contrast to the melodies that haunt the earlier selections. The brief “Drip” is its polar opposite, nearly a dance piece, restricted only by its length, the connecting tissue a feedback drone emerging toward the end. “Tide,” by far the album’s longest piece at 11:37, is dedicated to Christine Ödlund’s painting “Dissolving Strawberry,” and is also on a compilation EP that finds connections between pigment and tone. While listening, one gleans melodies through gauze, origins obscured like fragments of forgotten lyrics. By “How Far?” abstraction begins to win over form, Lewis’ voice suddenly emerging in the center as another instrument. Furthering the sense of inversion, the set closer is called “Opening,” making one wonder if the title may mean an opening, such as a pathway or door; or the sense of opening one’s self to unpredictability or the divine. By the time the album ends, one has been led down multiple pathways, and even the trail of string has become tangled. To find one’s bearings, one must return to the beginning or plunge further into the unknown. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Most ingredients are well known, but it’s the ingenuity with which they are married into one homogenous alloy that makes Anemoia not simply a standout IDM piece in terms of production proficiency and storytelling, but an important milestone in the history of modern electronic music in general and, for me, a present and future classic. Sonic royalty draped in mastery Anemoia by Ruxpin   I first “met” Ruxpin in the crevasses of a mixtape given to me by my good friend and techno DJ Katia in Zurich sometime in the late summer of 2005 or 2006. She had quickly become a stalwart for deep musical discovery at a rate that would still beat any music search algorithm today. She was especially passionate about a small niche of Icelandic producers who were little known on the European mainland, but who were presenting a very consistent, high-quality output, spreading their goodness on such acclaimed labels as Mikrolux (an Electrolux sub-label) and Uni and the like. I, on the other hand, being ignorant of Ruxpin, was instantly taken, and the intricate sonic layers made a deep impression on my then-IDM-obsessed self, which was chasing abstruse and more involved electronic tunes that sought to make an effort of transgressing the hyper-abstract polyrhythmic lore that had become so en vogue. This impression was deepened when I decided to spend New Year’s of the same year in Iceland with an old college friend and actually met Jonas, aka Ruxpin, in person at what can only be called one of the most random parties of my lifetime. Jonas instantly struck me as a young man with almost suspicious humility but a very clear, ingenious edge, who could not really be bothered with high acclaim and was instead completely focused on channeling his music from a deeper place. Iceland is a territory of particular wild beauty, but never more so than in the depth of what seemed to me like a winter of prehistoric dimensions. A lot has been said about how environments shape artistic output, and while I agree that this seems to be the case, I don’t think that this holds true to the content of the art, but merely to its form and modality. And Jonas’ music bears testimony to this suspicion. This 13-course meal is meant to be savored in its entirety :: 2003’s Magrathea and Elysium, which followed three years later, are not cold by nature, or bare like the outskirts of Reykjavík, even though a first listen might mislead one into becoming stuck with this impression. While they relate the image of technology-driven sonic narratives and insular grit, there is always a tender spark present. Just as I recall Jonas to be a warm and outspoken true artist who chooses his instruments to support his vision and not to become it, there is an undertone of extreme humaneness and delicate embellishment that sets him apart from the IDM predicament of static technocracy. The sub-genre “melodic IDM,” chosen by a variety of digital platforms to index him, is in my view a deceptive misnomer. To me, a more fitting category reads “emotionally intelligent dance music,” and I would largely award Ruxpin the entire category, as such a combination is as rare as common sense in American politics nowadays. As the news of a new full-length Ruxpin album titled Anemoia stumbled into my inbox, I was not only hit with extreme nostalgia and anticipation, but also met with slight terror. Because, as we all have experienced, many good things of former days have shown a tendency of undoing themselves. But just as Jonas had proven the quote “never meet your heroes” wrong, he also dismantled the suspicion that an IDM career cannot be successfully maintained without the loss of identity and quality over such a long period of time. Anemoia is not only a successful continuation of his lineage; it stands on its very own solid feet. At 13 tracks and just under one hour of runtime, this is no lightweight, but the music presented here defies gravity and weight measurements altogether. As a conceptual thinker, I like to attach my sense of an album around a central image. The one I would choose for Anemoia is that of abstract weightlessness, of a heavy landscape that stands suspended, not only in space but also in time. There is a sense of complementary opposition between heavy rolling beats and lofty pads that pervades all the tracks.   The magician the world needs him to be :: Yet another observation must be made. One that is not specific to Anemoia, but to Ruxpin in general: this is a closed-off, integrated and wholesome oeuvre. Breaking it down into individual tracks and noting their individual ingredients and how they stack up against each other is not only doing it a grave disservice, it’s misunderstanding Ruxpin. This 13-course meal is meant to be savored in its entirety, with only brief interruptions to permit one not to lose themselves completely. But even so, this is a canon of high specificity. It is unlike what Jonas presented before, even if his penmanship is clearly identifiable behind every single one of the clearly intentionally designed sounds. These tracks speak of maturing, of a coming of age, and of a homecoming of an artist who has survived the archetypes of warriorship and martyrdom and who is finally the magician the world needs him to be. There are clear traces of inspiration all over this. Crunchy hip-hop beats and even groovy house chords are spun around delicate arpeggios and staccatos that are well known to the IDM crowd, but in their execution, they seem oddly fresh and renewed, reinterpreted in a form that goes far beyond slinging your drum sounds through a 12-bit sampler or an SP-1200 DAC and calling it a day. No, this is about the conscious use of space and how to fill it. Jonas is a master at filling the canvas without overdoing it, at making density seem empty, at giving gas a weight, and turning time into a volume. While many IDM tracks are burdened by the “all buttons in” obsession, Anemoia remains easy without becoming anemic. Glitches and ratcheting never overtake, but are neatly tucked into a mix that has reached masterclass level. A master at filling the canvas without overdoing it :: Particular mention must be given to what has become a standout sound in his productions: the snare drum, or rather the sophisticated modulation thereof. Snares are difficult sounds that lesser experienced producers treat with a criminal lack of attention. On Anemoia, snares seem to carry much of the load and take on much of the duty usually attributed to the kick drum or entire percussion groups. Ruxpin does so effortlessly, but obviously with very great care, and one has to pay close attention to hear how these sounds take on a life of their own over the course of a track. In line with my sentiment that one should not discuss Anemoia as a collection of tracks but as a closed opus, I cannot identify a favorite. All of it seems relevant to the multi-tiered journey. To the point where I would fear that if one was to do the modern thing and only drag one track into their playlist, they would lose 80% of the essence contained and thin the momentum to a mere trickle. What might be a disadvantage to the modern music consumer seeking a quick fix between heavy compression algorithms and heterogeneous, anonymous track lists is a strong selling point for those interested in listening to bodies of work that are woven around storylines that contain the author’s essence and speak of their obsessive despair in rendering an inner vision into a DAW timeline. Yet none of this is to say that the tracks don’t contain life on their own. On the contrary. Just like any good movie scene must move the plot forward, everything is indeed in its right place, and Anemoia convinces with a very effective way of building, sustaining and eventually dissipating energy within every single track, at the microscopic as well as the macroscopic level. For example, “Seduction,” the entry into the album, as well as the two tracks “Aftermath” and “Setting the Sun” leading out of it, are the only ones that don’t greet the listener with an immediate swell of sizzling beats, but instead rely on signature chord stabs and bubbling pads. And “Pleasure Unit feat. Stafraenn Hakon” anchors the LP in its middle with a decidedly stomping march beat that comes as close to being an earworm as Ruxpin will permit.   A common sphere of universal musical wisdom :: There are moments within the journey that are reminiscent of “documentary braindance” and which evoke Boards of Canada-esque nostalgia, relaying a distinct Ektachrome feel because they hit the human brain in the exact same spot. Perhaps another reason why I was so quick to fall in love with its color palette. In a Jungian sense, this album relies, consciously or not, on the existence of artistic archetypes or mood boards, which it shares with other representatives and which take those attuned to it into similar distant terrains. All of this is much more a testament to Ruxpin’s ability to paint with a variety of synesthetic hues than a reductionist approach that borrows out of lack of originality. Akin to my own perspective on what art is, he seems to carve out of a common sphere of universal musical wisdom, rather than create from clay. Most ingredients are well known, but it’s the ingenuity with which they are married into one homogenous alloy that makes Anemoia not simply a standout IDM piece in terms of production proficiency and storytelling, but an important milestone in the history of modern electronic music in general and, for me, a present and future classic. This is sonic royalty draped in mastery. The eclectic electronic producer Ruxpin is one of the leading figures in Iceland’s contemporary electronic music scene. Widely associated with iconic labels such as n5MD and Elektrolux, Ruxpin has stayed true to his roots while continuously evolving his interpretation of melodic IDM, integrating soul and innovation into his music.Now based in Estonia, the artist was born and raised in Kópavogur, Iceland, and became involved in the electronic music scene at an early age. His first release came when he was just fifteen, followed two years later by his debut album on the Icelandic label Uni Recordings. The album received critical acclaim and caught the attention of German label Elektrolux, where he subsequently released his next four full-length albums. Since 2009, Ruxpin has released his work on Móatún 7, Sound In Silence, Ravekjavik, OMNIDISC, Sun Sea Sky, and n5MD. His latest release, however, comes courtesy of Martin Boulton’s Touched Music label.Anemoia is dedicated to Futuregrapher (RIP). Anemoia is available on Touched Music. items.body: Live in Brooklyn, 1992-2002 opens a decade-long aperture through which sound flees its dates and resumes its unfinished conversation with the present. Guitarist Jeffrey Schanzer and pianist-composer Bernadette Speach turn performance into a social form where individual voices ply dreams that are startlingly alive. The duo began collaborating in Buffalo in 1982, joining free jazz and global traditions to the post-Cagean avant-garde. After moving to Brooklyn two years later, they entered an artist-led culture sustained by collective labor. Schanzer served as president of the Musicians of Brooklyn Initiative, founded by Lester Bowie and Oliver Lake with Cecil Taylor; Speach worked as a producer and organizer. When MOBI closed, the pair co-founded MusicVistas, Inc., presenting concerts at Lafayette Presbyterian Church and the Brooklyn Society for Ethical Culture. The guests of those concerts, generously represented here in a selection spanning two discs, reveal a breadth of talent that includes Bowie and Lake, Wadada Leo Smith, Joseph Jarman, Leroy Jenkins, Mark Dresser, Fred Lonberg-Holm, and Alva Rogers. Yet the album resists becoming a parade of illustrious names. Its deepest subject is relation itself, the difficult art of remaining singular while entering another person’s orbit. The open improvisations expose that ethos, each encounter inventing its laws while obeying the fragile discipline of listening. With Lake on alto saxophone, Schanzer and Speach establish a fractured pulse as the horn slips through apertures between intention and reflex. Calls arrive already altered by their responses as the music sheds one skin, only to discover another consciousness underneath. Dr. David Pleasant’s appearance takes a more tactile route. Schanzer strikes the guitar into an ancestral ambiguity while Speach plucks the piano’s interior with aqueous precision. Pleasant’s flute wanders as a spirit negotiating the burden of embodiment, and percussive impacts press against the music’s transparent membrane until fracture becomes illumination. The improvisation with Dresser descends into darker psychic matter. His arco bass draws a vibrating inquiry from an immeasurable well, while scraped textures worry the border between injury and knowledge. Pizzicato attacks bend ordinary hearing. Another improvisation, with Bowie and cellist Fred Lonberg-Holm, replaces abrasion with guarded tenderness. The musicians circle one another through reverb, protecting the work’s secrets from interpretation’s blunt appetite. Jenkins brings ferocious motion. His violin becomes the charged intelligence of a hive mind, agitating guitar and piano into radiance and unease. Beauty here carries no obligation to console. The composed works give these energies names without containing them. On Bowie’s “The Villager,” piano and guitar form a deep foundation for a trumpet voice at once incisive and grief-stricken. Bowie cuts through self-doubt by uncovering the harder question beneath it: What kind of survival leaves the soul intact? His tone pierces without cruelty, and the duo follows its eastern-facing thread into a region where mourning acquires sinews. Smith’s “Rain Flowers, Vertical Spears and Diamond Sunrays,” stretching beyond 24 minutes, is the collection’s vastest chamber of metamorphosis. His koto extends touch itself, entwining with Schanzer’s guitar until chronology folds in on itself. Speach’s toy piano releases tiny constellations over the full instrument’s historical resume. Smith’s muted trumpet seems peeled from an antique surface, its metallic cry approaching a bowed gong’s resonance. Alva Rogers’s “Foreign Affair” turns the album toward the politics of the body. Over Schanzer and Speach’s lush harmonic ground, the composer moves between speech and song, granting each word a physical contour. Her urban narrative of encounter and self-possession refuses the body’s reduction to currency. Desire becomes sovereign, alert to every mechanism that would classify or discard it. In “Glove Quartet,” Holland Hopson’s soprano saxophone and electronics meet John J.A> Jannone’s circuitry and Schanzer’s aggressive electric guitar. The surfaces grow harder, but lyricism keeps opening hidden doors in the machinery. Jarman’s “Hollows Five: II – Sincere Words. Can’t Compromise or Overpower” offers the most immersive ritual. Bells and bowls summon depth without exoticizing it; piano and guitar locate pressure points within the surrounding network. Jarman’s flute and alto saxophone carry a restless human shade through recurring figures. Brooklyn’s so-called second renaissance took material form. It required rooms, organizers, trust, and the stubborn conviction that art could build forms of civic life unavailable elsewhere. Schanzer and Speach hoped these recordings would transport listeners to that place and time. They accomplish something stranger. The album makes the past responsible to the future, asking whether listening can become a moral practice rather than private consumption. Within these performances, freedom means the exacting effort of making space for another consciousness without furnishing that space in advance. Perhaps the archive ultimately exceeds remembrance and becomes a score for communities that do not yet exist, waiting inside us for the courage to become audible. The post Schanzer/Speach Duo with guests: Live in Brooklyn, 1992-2002 appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — This has been sat in my playlist for well over a year by this point. I've heard it many times, but when it comes to writing a review about it, I have no idea what to say, or how to start. So here's the lowdown, released in 2005, 'The 1st Chapter' is the debut album by Norwegian progressive metal band, Circus Maximus. That's pretty much all there is to it. It's a solid album, which ticks off all the prog metal clich�s; fantastic musicianship, a singer with a powerful voice who can hit incredibly high notes, long, intricate song structures, and thoughtful, introspective lyrics. It's all here. One thing I struggled with is that there's nothing that specifically stands out that I can comment on. The music is really good and well produced, sounding a lot like Dream Theater or Symphony X (obviously), which is standard for this genre. In fact, there is one absolutely fantastic track, 'Glory of the Empire', which sounds like it could have come off of Symphony X's album 'The Odyssey', so if you like that album, you'll love this! The lyrics even have the legendary Gladiator line about "what happens in life echoes in eternity". You know the one. The absolute cheek of them! Still, lack of enthusiasm aside for my review, this is a good album. 'Sin', 'Why Am I Here', 'Biosfear', bonus track 'Haunted Dreams' and the aforementioned '?Empire' song are all worth checking out, and I've no doubt that Circus Maximus will stand out a lot more with subsequent releases.

items.body: Review by ianjferris@gmail.com — So, right now, I'm wondering if I'm one of those "completionists" that I read about every so often; those people who just have to have everything that a band releases into the marketplace. Is that the reason that I own this album? Because when I read down through the twelve strong tracklist thereupon, I clearly see that I have exatly nine of these exact tracks on other official album releases - "Live At Knebworth", "PULSE", "Delicate Sound of Thunder" and "A Momentary Lapse Of Reason remix". The three tracks that I don't have (or should I more correctly say, the versions of those three tracks that appear here which I don't already have) are, "Marooned Jam" from The Division Bell Sessions, "Lost For Words" taken from a PULSE Tour rehearsal and an early version of "High Hopes" from the Division Bell Sessions. Of course I do have all three substantive versions of these tracks on their original album releases. So back to my original musings, am I a "completionist". No, I'm not. This is a compilation album, which brings together here twelve excellent pieces which, if I wished to hear them and them alone without this album, I'd have to fooster around selecting from different albums that I have on the shelf. I put this album on every so often specifically because these tracks are the ones that I want to hear. And a small bonus (very small bonus) is the fact that a version of three of the twelve are not available to me in my collection. So, conclusion..... I'm not a "completionist". I'm an ordinary fan who loves this compilation and I'm giving it five stars because that is what this music deserves.

items.body: Review by omphaloskepsis — When I picture the Mount Rushmore of Chamber Prog, I clearly see the colossal Universe Zero and Present rising above a foggy valley, carved into the mountain side. The thick mist of time obscures the other etched visages jutting from the far-side of the Mountain. The Fool Leading The Blind amazes me and I wonder..."Will Asceta approach Univers Zero and Present's greatness? Time will tell. Asceta's album The Fool Leading the Blind is a resplendent, melodic, and focused masterpiece of modern chamber rock and Rock in Opposition (RIO). The epic tapestry, fashioned by multi-instrumentalist and composer Rodrigo Maccioni, the Chilean ensemble crafts an intricate sound shroud knit together with awesome, seamless transitions. Bassoon, clarinets, viola, and English horn merge with a jazzy electric guitars, bass, and drums. Asceta's music doesn't percolate with as many dissonate passages as Univers Zero or Present. Don't get me wrong, Asceta sails through its share of breathtaking dissonate rapids. However, Asceta's The Fool Leading The Blind seems more focused on melodic movements...much like classical compositions from a couple centuries ago.The Title Suite: The opening 21-minute epic flows fluidly from eerie, atmospheric sound spheres to exhilarating crescendos. The dynamic Interplay of tracks like Temple of Mirrors and When They Arrive showcase tight counterpoints where no single instrument dominates, weaving impeccable sonic tapestries into complex patterns. Every track is a treat! Asceta's thought-provoking, sonic bouquet shimmers like shattered stain glass in a cathedral on fire. Highly recommended for lovers of Univers Zero and Present.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As soon as you start listening to Quickly Quickly Quickly, and their opening track, "Firebears", you are plunged into a sonic explosion you weren't prepared for; it is a surprise that stirs you in much the same way hearing classic 70s bands for the first time did. I was reminded of King Crimson, there is something epic about it, yet also dark and dangerous, and yet I also thought of Sonic Youth, who, incidentally, also feature two guitarists, a crucial element in creating that sonic canvas.The way the keyboards and guitars intertwine was also innovative, and that was nothing compared to what followed, as the McGowan brothers sing with such deep emotion and grit. This sets them apart from other bands that might be solid instrumentally but, at least to my ears, lack a distinctive signature. The arrangements constantly shift and adapt to the unfolding music, a progression that is hard to predict, with the vocals guiding the instruments as they collectively build the melody, reversing the usual dynamic.Contrasts emerge quickly; a more introspective section takes on a nearly jazzy feel, albeit indirectly, and the piano can be as laid-back as Neil Young during the moments when Crazy Horse was resting. Towards the end, at times I thought I heard the voice of Chris Cornell from Soundgarden, specifically during his band's psychedelic moments, and I found that same powerful vocal range, imbued with genuine emotion, once again in The Tea Club."The Eternal German Infant" presents a contrast between its instrumental power, a kind of restrained violence, and the vulnerability of the vocals; it then plunges into imagery woven from seemingly disjointed guitar, bass, and keyboard notes, with the guitar tearing at notes as if seeking a meeting point between the spirit of the voice and the music, a near-theatrical encounter."Mister Freeze" opens another door within the established framework, that dreamlike (or perhaps nightmarish) atmosphere, as if hundreds of crystal shards were parting to clear the way: an acoustic guitar paired with electric strumming that hangs like a curtain of stained glass catching the sunlight. The same notes repeat, yet with a certain decomposition, like fruit left too long in the summer sun. The subtlety of David Sylvian's solo work gains ground, casting a protective mantle, that sheltering sky spoken of by writer Paul Bowles, evoking a desert soundtrack: the organ, the strumming guitar... and one mask concealing another."I Shall Consume Everything" layers on intensity, steadily building tension; drums and a guitar join the keyboards, shifting from the style of the early Fripp (circa 1969) to the Greek echoes of Aphrodite's Child, until a guitar riff finally tears down what was built, driven by distortion, overlapping and repeating vocals, and rhythmic breaks that shatter the melody, causing it to quickly fade away......was any disintegration worthy of the name ever slow?

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One might associate Chile with the folk songs of V�ctor Jara, the psychedelic and progressive past of Los Jaivas, or high-quality pop-rock bands like La Ley; yet Cherc�n offers a pleasant surprise with a bold, distinctive rock sound that draws from psychedelia while incorporating a jazz-infused saxophone and string arrangements, featuring violin and cello, that add nuance to the quintet's (and its guests') fast-paced progressive rock style."La culpa" is the opening track, reminiscent of The Mars Volta in its wild, defiant nature, where the sound builds toward a final climax, intensifying as if funneling through the guitar; the audio distorts while Mart�n Pe�a, the vocalist, belts out vocals that are at once melodic and visceral. There are moments of great freedom, reminiscent of jazz scat singing, that shift into free-jazz passages blended with hard rock. This fusion, combined with the vocalist's delivery (which at times resembles a mystical, inverted prayer), reaches a new level of decibel intensity and opens up a new dimension for the saxophone within progressive heavy rock, distinct from the styles of Van der Graaf Generator (a feat that once seemed impossible) or Gong, two major touchstones for the instrument in this genre. Here, the fusion is more contemporary, yet Kalimba still retains melody and harmony, in abundance, while incorporating folk influences drawn from indigenous music.The instrumental sections still sound as improvised and fresh as when they must have been composed; when the band kicks into highly intricate, distorted rock, backed by the string section, the music gains added weight without losing any power; quite the opposite. Mart�n Pe�a holds his own as a vocalist, knowing exactly how to function as yet another instrument.Tiempos paralelos can serve as a summary of Cherc�n's musical approach, as the first part involves the saxophone and a sense of restraint, while the second features an uprising led by the guitar and a defiant vocal performance, delivering a solo reminiscent of Annie Haslam channeling Ian Gillan. "Las Mentiras del Muro" opens with a powerful foundation of drums and bass that reminded me of the overflowing energy of Rage Against the Machine, though the comparison stops at the vocals, as Mart�n Pe�a handles both the metal and progressive sections with the same care and precision found in the saxophone notes; the sax, for all its delicacy, sounds no less powerful and truly stands out as a key protagonist of the album."Relato de una obsesi�n", specifically its first part, titled "Quimera", features Eastern percussion and rhythms; the quintet achieves such a profound communion that they seem to act as one, wholly absorbed in the task of capturing their vision for posterity. The second part, "El orate," erupts, unleashing the inevitable, a tidal surge that can no longer be contained. It embodies that Eastern-inspired tensi�n, held taut to the point of infinity, until it finally meets the resistance it had ultimately sought, and that fiery blaze, which was in fact its very reason for being, is consumed.As if the ashes still held light and heat after the fire, the album's final track, "Colores," embodies a mysticism that retains its clarity, refusing to be blinded by its own nature, and one that learns and evolves, promising a future that will harvest the seeds sown in this auspicious debut.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — "Have one on Me" appeared 4 years after the landmark "Ys", with part of the delay relating to nodules on the singer's vocal cords in 2009 induced no doubt in part by her untrained and untamed pipes. Perhaps in reaction to her improved health and in an attempt not to repeat the same mistakes too quickly, this triple album of 3 LP length parts highlights more instrumental acumen, that is to say, it actually has breaks where she rests her voice, and some are the highlights of their respective tracks, indeed sometimes the only redeeming feature on the likes of "Good Intentions Paving Co". Joanna also sings in a more classically skilled manner without abandoning that whimsy entirely, even piling vocalise on the aforementioned and the title cut. These modifications coincide with and even steer the production into rock and jazz realms in preference to the chambered directives of the pre nodular Joanna. Merged with a handful of her best tunes- "'81", "Baby Birch", "On a Good Day", "In California", "Go Long" and "Kingfisher" - it's worth toasting (along with her health) if not wholeheartedly lionizing.

items.body: Mezzo-soprano Aigul Akhmetshina has sung her fair share of notable female characters—femmes fatales like Carmen (Carmen) and Dalila (Samson et Dalila), and others more innocent like Angelina (La Cenerentola) or Olga (Eugene Onegin). Her newest project with Antonio Pappano on piano, Mujer Fatal, is a multifaceted commentary on womanhood. Mujer Fatal Amazon Presto Apple The program ranges well beyond the operatic repertoire, and the mix proves attractive. It opens with the title track, written specifically for Akhmetshina by Elena Roussanova and recorded here for the first time. Both singer and pianist express the impassioned side of the femme fatale, but Akhmetshina adds an unmistakable fearlessness as well. In the song’s middle section she gives us glimpses of its opposite: vulnerability. The two featured songs from Montsalvatge’s Canciones negras speak to Akhmetshina’s technique: nothing overtly flashy, but a clarity of pitch and diction that carries No. 1 (track 2). Her breath control in No. 4 (track 3) yields long, luxurious legato lines. The songs are well-paired, setting yearning against dreaming. Bésame mucho (track 6) is the most recognizable of the non-classical offerings. Jonathan Palmer Lakeland’s arrangement of Consuelo Velázquez’s bolero affords the singer a spotlight that she maximizes: her phrases are lithe and organic, and even when the piano introduces a more structured rhythmic accompaniment, she upholds the sultry air that is central to the song. Ravel‘s Pièce en forme de Habanera (track 8) is one of the most impressive tracks for its expressive and technical range. As with many of his works, the difficulty is hidden in the finer details, and such is the case here: the melismatic passages are tightly controlled yet come off as spontaneous. Several moments of pointed interjection from the duo surprise not because they are out of place, but because they push past the expected emotional intensity. Given the minimalism of some of his best-known piano works, Erik Satie and his Je te veux (track 9) reveal a very different side, one that the duo portrays effectively. The music here is decidedly emotive, at times even rhapsodic. Through the drama, we can appreciate the persuasiveness of Akhmetshina’s sweeping vocal lines. Tchaikovsky‘s None but the Lonely Heart (track 11) possesses a similar earnestness and gives Pappano a chance to shine. Compared to some of the other songs, the keyboard has a greater presence here, and it is a pleasure to hear Pappano and Akhmetshina in a well-informed partnership: the lines intertwine at times, but one never feels in the way of the other. Rimsky-Korsakov’s The Nightingale and the Rose (track 12) carries a sense of mystery in its opening piano interlude; Akhmetshina’s first solo, unaccompanied, builds further tension and suspense. One of the most striking aspects of the song is the sheer vocal range required, and she shows complete comfort capturing the piercing high notes as she evokes the quiet enigma of the lower ones. Aigul Akhmetshina. Photo © Lera Nurgalieva. Of the American selections, those from Gershwin and Bernstein stand out. The Man I Love (track 14) juxtaposes Pappano’s jazzy yet pensive suavity with Akhmetshina’s sumptuous timbre. While her singing does come off a little heavy-handed at times, it does justice to the meaning of the text. Somewhere (track 16) sees Akhmetshina at her most sensitive in a comforting reading. A serious issue with the digital version of the album is that it does not come with a booklet, which, in a program like this, is paramount for song texts and translations. The physical CD appears to include them. This misstep aside, the performances are exquisite and make a convincing case for Akhmetshina and Pappano’s artistic versatility. If you enjoyed this album, also hear Aigul Akhmetshina: Aigul | Joyce DiDonato: Songplay | Elīna Garanča: Sol y Vida | Isabel Leonard & Sharon Isbin: Alma Española The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: This is French cellist Astrig Siranossian’s fifth release on the Alpha label, and her earlier albums cover a wide-ranging repertoire in which she appears both as a chamber musician and as a soloist. Here she is joined by the London Symphony Orchestra and François-Xavier Roth for Elgar’s Cello Concerto, with Britten’s Cello Sonata, Bruch’s Kol Nidrei and Elgar’s Salut d’amour completing the program. Cello Concerto Amazon Presto Apple There are some ninety readily available recordings of the Elgar Cello Concerto, so Siranossian is entering a crowded field. Every new release is measured against Jacqueline du Pré’s legendary performance with Barbirolli and the LSO (Warner Classics), and that status is well earned — I know of few other concerto recordings in which the solo part is played with such overwhelmingly personal, emotional expression. Barbirolli’s accompaniment is just as involving. But it is fascinating to hear Elgar’s own 1928 recording with Beatrice Harrison (the composer conducting the New Symphony Orchestra, Warner Classics), where his less heart-on-sleeve leadership has a different but potent emotional effect. Recent performances tend to fall into two contrasting interpretive camps. Some are gentler and more emotionally restrained, such as Paul Watkins/BBC Philharmonic/Davis (Chandos), Gautier Capuçon/LSO/Pappano (Erato), and Daniel Müller-Schott/Oslo Philharmonic/Previn (Orfeo). Others embrace a more extroverted emotional approach like du Pré’s that is nevertheless their own, such as Pieter Wispelwey/Netherlands Radio Philharmonic/van Steen (Channel Classics), Steven Isserlis/Philharmonia/Paavo Järvi (Hyperion), and Johannes Moser/Suisse Romande/Manze (Pentatone). Siranossian’s interpretation falls into the latter category. Her playing, caught up close by Alpha’s engineers, draws a dazzling range of colors from the 1756 Gennaro Gagliano cello. Siranossian’s interpretive ideal is signaled in the opening recitative: marked fortissimo and nobilmente, the initial attack is ferocious and emotionally raw, the nobilmente honored through color and weight rather than any stiff-upper-lip reticence. Her first statement of the main theme is silvery and lithe, while the later restatement is full-toned and impassioned. The second movement (Lento – Allegro molto) brings a delicate, playful lightening of mood, answered by an Adagio of greater intensity, the playing more inward and contemplative, the cello’s color at times blanched and exhausted. The final movement returns to a more unreserved, impassioned manner, surveying darker regions of the score that others leave unexplored. The LSO, which has played this score more times than anyone can count, strives to match Siranossian’s intensity, but is sometimes hampered by Roth’s more objective leadership. There is compensation in hearing the score laid out with such transparency, allowing us to appreciate the craft of Elgar’s writing. Astrig Siranossian. I last wrote about Britten‘s Cello Sonata in a review of Sheku Kanneh-Mason’s 2025 Decca recording. That reading, like this one from Siranossian and pianist Nathanaël Gouin, a regular duo partner, leans into the tough modernity of Britten’s writing. If the Kanneh-Mason siblings find more playfulness in the second-movement Scherzo, Siranossian and Gouin more thoroughly uncover the darker musings of the third-movement Elegia, albeit at a significantly faster tempo. The Marcia lacks the menace Johannes Moser finds (with pianist Paul Rivinius, Hänssler), but the closing Moto perpetuo has ferocious momentum and drive, without eclipsing the unique energy and bravado of Rostropovich’s account with the composer (Decca). Bruch‘s Kol Nidrei is built around two Jewish melodies. The composer described the first as “an age-old Hebrew song of atonement”; the second, in D major, draws on “O weep for those that wept on Babel’s stream,” a song he called moving and truly magnificent. The only performance of the work I own is János Starker’s with the LSO led by Doráti (Eloquence). It is quite lovely, both pained and calming. Siranossian’s slightly slower reading is more sweetly voiced and more openly poignant. Elgar’s Salut d’amour makes a perfect digestif. Alpha’s engineering is excellent, and it is particularly good to hear the LSO away from the acoustically challenged Barbican Hall; the concerto sessions took place at LSO St Luke’s. The liner notes consist of a January 2026 interview in which Siranossian spends more time on what connects her cello (once owned by John Barbirolli) with the repertoire on the album than on the music itself. Nevertheless, after hearing this recording I intend to hear Siranossian’s earlier albums — recommended. items.body: And so, as summer draws to a close and we enter the ever-popular fall season (which affords us the use of the word “autumnal”, which you fucking bet we’ll be working in wherever possible), we also enter the final third of 2026. Of course, needing to get our Year End coverage done and dusted by mid-December means we’ve got roughly three months left of coverage, and the actual determination of what records we liked the most still to come. As always, suggestions of things we’ve overlooked are always welcome, as are your own picks, feel free to toss ’em in the comments below. But of course, this is all a preamble for our most venerable tradition, ye olde Tracks post. Join us won’t you? Creux Lies Pig, “An American Ideal of Beauty” Raymond Watts sure is a busy guy these days. Aside from a massive tour he’s kicking off across North America, the Pig mastermind is following up this year’s enjoyable Hurt People Hurt with a smattering of follow-up EPs. The first of those, from which the track embedded below is taken, is Dirt Box, featuring four new tracks with accompanying remixes by the likes of Stabbing Westward, Combichrist, Cyanotic and Rabbit Junk. Then we’ve got Merciless coming down the pike, a remix EP with cuts by Clock DVA (!!) and Pitchshifter amongst others. I guess you can’t keep a good hog down. Dirt Box by PIG Creux Lies, “Jubilate” Man, but Sacramento’s Creux Lies are keeping us on our toes. The depth and richness of sophomore LP Goodbye Divine has us waiting on a follow-up with bated breath, but the third original track they’ve released over the past couple of years sounds very distinct from its predecessors. Here, they’re in an easily approachable synth dancefloor mode, but the real sauce is in the slowburn approach Ean Elliot Clevenger takes to the vocals which build across its runtime. Jubilate by Creux Lies UNTER STRØM, “Stumbling” UNTER STRØM is the side-project of Alex from LA’s post-punkers Matte Blvck, and while it is a more down the pipe electronic project than its parent band, it’s a far cry from the defacto sound of modern electro-darkwave. Indeed, while the sound of their material is certainly of a more shadowy cast, you’re getting programming and arrangements that refer to more aboveground sounds in the world of progressive house and melodic techno, splitting the difference between those bright club nights and dark underground dancefloors in fine fashion. Between Forms by UNTER STRØM alarm!systemen, “Burn” Don’t let the apparent compositional simplicity of Belgian newcomers alarm!systemen’s approach to melancholy coldwave on this track fool you; there’s a real consideration of colour and harmony here which makes a virtue of modern gear and technique rather than eschewing it for the sage of nostalgia, while shooting a style familiar to fans of any number of early 80s continental acts with a bright and fresh strain of dreampop. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Evil Dust, “Sadistic” Some good n’ gnarly lo-fi business from London body music act Evil Dust, whose new LP I Just Want to Fit In is due shortly on the 11th of September. If’n you like some of the stuff that the whole industrialized techno sound was doing, but wish it was, well, more industrial, this might fit the bill; heavily percussive, lots of sample work, and an unruly groove that never quite settles in where you think it will. I JUST WANT TO FIT IN by EVIL DUST Einhänder Aus Stahl, “4 Meter Punch To The Face (Visitor remix)” Speaking of lo-fi body music, the new maxi EP from Einhänder Aus Stahl, the side project of Micheal of Chrome Corps, offers a slew of minimal tracks which strip throwback techno and EBM to their barest skeleton. Throw in a little bit of left-field synth-funk courtesy of Visitor (you probably don’t need us to ID the samples for you) and you have a twitchy, burpy blast of fun. items.body: The whispers in my mind, the echoes of my past, Judgment in the mirror, a reflection that will last. The mind can build a courtroom from almost nothing. A remembered phrase becomes evidence, an old mistake is summoned as a witness, and conscience takes the prosecutor’s table before crossing the room to pronounce sentence from the bench. No counsel appears for the defense, no statute of limitations applies, and every hour spent alone provides another opportunity to reopen the case. On Up Against the Wall, Minsk-based artist Tomorrows Letters turns this internal proceeding into a severe and stylish piece of noir synthpop. The solo project of Kiryl Karotki, Tomorrows Letters enters the song already cornered, facing a tribunal in which the accused, prosecutor, and judge occupy the same body. A low, saxophone-like drone opens the recording before giving way to a mechanized groove. Sparse piano notes land beside Karotki’s controlled vocal, lending each phrase the gravity of sworn testimony. His delivery remains cold and composed, yet there is considerable force beneath that restraint, like silk draped across the song’s dread. Trip-hop menace and industrial textures run through the rhythm, meeting the darker electronic pop associated with Depeche Mode’s 1990s and early-2000s records. The clipped construction also carries the severe elegance of 1980s new wave and minimal synth. When the saxophone returns between verses, it winds through organ-like keys and a low electronic buzz, giving the track the character of a neo-noir jazz performance conducted inside a machine. Karotki’s voice completes the setting, transporting the listener into a room filled with stark light, suspended haze, and hard silhouettes. Every word appears carefully measured, as though an answer given too quickly could become further evidence for the prosecution. The lyrics make this psychological trial explicit. Past mistakes supply the testimony, the mirror preserves the verdict, and the heartbeat keeps time for fear. Within the “courtroom of my soul,” the singer bears every role and pays every toll. By the outro, the narrow line between right and wrong has become another instrument of captivity: “I’m a prisoner of my own mind.” “The song describes a state where your own mind acts as both the prosecutor and the judge in a trial that never ends,” Karotki explains. “It’s about being your own worst enemy, trapped in a loop of self-judgment where conscience acts as a punisher rather than a moral guide.” The single release of Up Against the Wall, the first offering from Karotki’s debut LP set for release this autumn. It is accompanied by an exclusive remix from Karotki’s friends in Nürnberg, marking the first of several guest appearances and collaborations planned for the forthcoming album. The song was mixed and mastered by Nürnberg’s sound engineer, Andrei Bobrovka, while its cover artwork was created by Tomorrows Letters. Tomorrows Letters is a project that operates according to a strict hardware-only philosophy, with Karotki using vintage samplers and unconventional songwriting methods to give it a dusty, tactile character. New Romantic and minimal synth-pop influences provide the foundation, though their historical language is put in the service of present-day psychological estrangement. Across his work, Karotki examines isolation, self-judgment, Jungian ideas concerning the hidden self, maladaptive daydreaming, compulsive creation, and the pursuit of victories that prove empty once attained.
